summary: The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. The Income Tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee under section 4(1)(a) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957 on the ground that the assessee had not been able to prove his claim for deduction under section 5(2) of Wealth Tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount of Rs. 1,00,000 was a capital receipt and not a capital asset. On appeal by the Revenue, the Appellate Tribunal held that there was no evidence on record to show that the sum of Rs, 1,50,000 had been received by the assessee from the assessee in the course of his business. The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the Revenue that the High Court erred in holding that the capital asset was a revenue receipt and that the income was not a revenue asset. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding the assessee liable to be assessed under section 6(2)(a). [703 B] 2.2 In the instant case, the assessee was entitled to deduction under Section 5(3) of Act. The assessee had failed to prove that the amounts received by him were capital assets. The Revenue could not have claimed deduction under the Wealth tax Act. [704 C D] 3.1 In view of the fact that the Income Tax officer assessed the assessee for the purpose of computing the net wealth of the deceased in respect of the assessment year 1966 67, the High Courts erred in treating the amount as capital asset and not the income from the assets of the family. [774 E F] 2:2 The High court was right in taking a contrary view. [764 C] 3:3 In the case of an assessee who is assessed to wealth tax under section 7(1) (a), the assessee has to prove the claim for deductions under Section 4(2). [765 G H] 4:4. The question whether the amount received by a Hindu Undivided Family is capital asset or not does not arise in this case. [754 C D, F] 5:5. In view thereof, the Revenue could have claimed that the deduction under Sections 5(1), 5(4) and 6(3)(a), was a permissible deduction under sections 5(6) and 7(2), as it stood before the amendment of section 4 (1).

The respondent was a Head Constable in the Department of Personnel and Training, Government of India. He was promoted as Assistant Director (Civil) on ad hoc basis. He filed an appeal before the Central Administrative Tribunal, which dismissed his appeal. The Tribunal held that the respondent had not been given any opportunity to cross examine him. The respondent preferred an appeal against the order of dismissal. The High Court set aside the order and directed reinstatement of the respondent with full back wages. Aggrieved by the said order, the appellant has filed this appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal was right in holding that the charge against the respondent was proved beyond reasonable doubt. [775F] 2.2 In the instant case, the Tribunal had not given any reasons for its conclusion. The order of the Tribunal is set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal for fresh disposal on merits. [771G] 3.1 It is well settled that in a departmental proceeding, the Court has to be satisfied that there was no evidence or material before it to show that the charges were proved beyond doubt. In the present case, there was nothing to show as to how the respondent could have been given an opportunity to defend himself. The charge against him was not proved beyond any reasonable doubt and he had failed to prove that he had committed any misconduct. [761G H] 2:2 The Tribunal has not given reasons for his conclusion. It is not a case of gross violation of principles of natural justice. The findings recorded by the Tribunal are set aside. [753F G] 3:3 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it would be appropriate to interfere with the order passed by the Tribu nal. [781G; 771A B] 4:4 It is a well settled principle that in an departmental proceeding where there are two views on the evidence adduced before the Tribunal, one should not be allowed to be influenced by the other. The Court has no power to interfere in such findings unless it is shown that the conclusions are perverse or unreasonable. [ 771G G] 5:5 In the case of a departmental enquiry, the High Court has not recorded reasons for interfering with the finding of the Tribuna nal and the Tribunal has given reasons which are not germane for the decision of the t he case. The reasons given by the High Courts are set out in the order dated 25th September, 1987 passed by this Court in Union of India vs M.L. Sharma & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellants filed a suit for possession of the property in dispute on the ground that they were tenants under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable as the suit had been instituted within three years from the date of the institution of the suit. The High Court held that the plaintiff was entitled to possession of a property in suit for specific performance of contract and that the defendant was entitled only to possession on the basis of the lease deed executed by him. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The suit was barred by limitation as it was filed within three months from the institution thereof. [775G] 2.2 The suit is not maintainable because the plaintiff had no locus standi to file the suit in view of the provisions of section 7(3) of the Act. [774C D] 3.1 In a suit instituted by a tenant against the defendant for possession, the Court has to decide whether the plaintiff is entitled to the relief claimed by him or not. The Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit on the grounds that the claim was barred under section 7 of the Bombay Act. The plaintiff cannot be allowed to file a suit in respect of the same property. [764C] 3:2 In a proceeding instituted by the landlord against the tenant for possession against the defendants, the court has to determine whether the defendant is entitled or not and whether he was entitled or entitled to any relief claimed. If the plaintiff has no locus to file it, the question of limitation would be one of fact. [754C E] 3 :3 In a civil suit instituted in the Court of Civil Judge, Bombay, the plaintiff cannot claim any right to possession against him. The jurisdiction of the court is limited to the jurisdiction of a civil court and not to entertain a suit. If he has no such right, he can ask for a decree for possession on that ground alone. [744C F] 4:3 In the instant case, the suit filed by the plaintiff in respect thereof was barred because the defendant had not been given any notice of the date when the suit came up for hearing and the suit itself was barred. The suit filed in the year 1967 was therefore barred by time as it fell within the purview of section 2(1) of Bombay Act, and the plaintiff could not be allowed a decree on that basis. [784C G] 4.4 In the facts and circumstances of the case, there is no merit in the contention that the defendants were entitled to relief under section 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The defendant was not entitled to claim any relief under the Act because he had not filed a civil Suit in the Bombay High Court.

The petitioners are employees of the respondent Corporation. They were employed as a casual labour in the State of Himachal Pradesh. Their services were terminated by the Corporation on the ground that they had been engaged in the work of cleaning and cleaning of the food grains, and that they were not entitled to any salary for the period of their service. The petitioners contended that they are entitled to the salary for their work as a regular labour under the State Government. Their claim was rejected by the Labour Court on the grounds that they have been engaged as a temporary labour under a State Government and that the Corporation has no power to fix the pay scales of the employees of other departments. The writ petition filed by them was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the petitioners are entitled for the salary in terms of the Rules framed under the . It was further contended that the State Govern ment has no authority to fix their pay scales and that there is no discrimination between the employees and the employees. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The Corporation has been discharging its functions as a piece time measure measure measure and it has been entrusted with the task of ensuring the quality of work done by them. It has been established that the employees are entitled only to the pay scale of the workers employed in the establishment. [703B C] 2. The State Government has not made any rule for fixing the pay of the petitioners. The Court cannot interfere with the decision of the High Courts. [774C D] 3. The question whether the petitioners have been paid the salary of the respondents is a matter of policy and not one of fact. It is not necessary that the Court should be slow to interfere with it unless there are compelling reasons for doing so. [764F G] 4. The Supreme Court has laid down certain principles in regard to the fixation of pay scales, the nature of work performed by the employees, the manner in which they are employed and the manner of their recruitment. It cannot be said that the High court has not applied its mind to the question whether there is any discrimination between them or not. [754F] 5. The principle laid down in regard t he petitioners is not applicable to the case. The respondents have been discharging their duties as a daily rated worker and they are not entitled for salary for that period. They are entitled, therefore, to be paid the same scale of pay. [784C E] 6. The High Court has not considered the question of discrimination between employees and employees in the matter of fixing the scales of pay of their work. It was also not open to the petitioners to contend that they should be paid salary for each period of service. They have been denied the same benefit as they were working in the establishments. [ 774C] 7. The petitioner has not challenged the decision on the question as to whether the respondents are entitled or not, and the HighCourt has rightly held that the respondents have not been paid salary in lieu of the work done.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that they had been falsely implicated in the murder of one of the accused persons, and that the evidence of P.W. 1 was not corroborated by the evidence given by P.Ws. 2 and 3, who were eye witnesses to the occurrence, and convicted them under section 201 read with Section 34 of I.P.C., and sentenced them to death under section 304 Part II of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The State preferred an appeal against acquittal of all the appellants on the grounds that (1) there was no evidence to show that P. Ws. 2, 3 and 4 had been guilty of murder; (2) there were no eye witnesses in the occurrence; (3) there is no evidence that P.,Ws. 1 and 3 had been involved in the crime; (4) there are no eye witness to the incident; (5) there has been no motive for the accused to commit the murder; and (6) there could be no motive on the part of the prosecution to commit murder, and (7) there can be no doubt that P had been acquitted by the High Court. The conviction of all these appellants under section201 read with 34 of Indian Penal code was also upheld by this Court in appeal. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 There is no reason why the High court should not have interfered with the judgment of acquittal passed by the trial court. [730C] 2.2 The conviction and sentence under section 120B read with sections 34 and 201 readwith section 34 I. P.C. are set aside. [774G H; 730A B] 3.3 In the instant case, there is nothing to show in the evidence that the accused had been charged with murder or that he was convicted for murder. The prosecution has not proved that P, Ws. 1, 3, 4 and 5 were involved in any criminal act. [764G] 4.4 There is also no evidence on record to show how the accused were involved. It is true that there are two eye witnesses who have been examined by the prosecution, but they are not related to each other. But the evidence does not establish that P was involved in a criminal act and the accused was acquitted by any of the charges framed against them.

The appellant executed a will in favour of the respondent and his mother, who was the sole heir of the testator. The will was executed by the testator on the basis of the will. The appellant executed the will in her favour. The execution of the document was challenged by the appellant on the ground that it was not executed by her and that the will was not a genuine one. Held, that the execution of a will is a valid one and must be held to have been executed by a testator. It is well settled that the court has to look into the surrounding circumstances and find out whether the document is genuine or not. The onus lies on the propounder to prove that it is genuine and not merely on the other side. The burden of proving that the document had been executed in favour or was on the person who made the will, but the onus rests upon the propounder. The court has no power to examine the surrounding circumstance and find whether the testator had acted in good faith. It cannot be said that the testator has acted in a manner which is not permissible under section 100 of the Evidence Act. The mere fact that the executant was present at the time when the will came into existence, does not make it a case of fraud or collusion. The presumption of fraud and collusion is not conclusive. The propounder has to prove the circumstances before him. The Court cannot be expected to examine such circumstances as are necessary for the purpose of proving the fact that he had acted bona fide in good good faith and that he has acted bona fides in good conduct.

The appellant company was carrying on business in the manufacture of goods. The appellants were manufacturing and selling goods for the purpose of manufacturing and supplying goods. In the course of inter State trade, the appellants used to use the word "goods" as used in Entry 52 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. They used to import the word 'goods" in Entry 54 of List I of the VII Schedule to that Act. The High Court held that the word was not a mere device to cover all kinds of goods and that the use of the word did not amount to manufacture within the meaning of Entry 52, List II. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'sale" in entry 52 is used in the sense of "goods". It is used as a means for the purposes of manufacturing or supplying goods and it is used only as a device to prevent the use. [601B C] 2. The expression "goods", in Entry 53, List I, has been defined in Entry 51 of List III. In entry 52, the word has been used in entry 54 of list II. It means that the words "any goods" are used in a sense which includes all kinds or things including those mentioned therein. [701B D] 3. The use of word 'business" is not defined in the Act. Entry 52 does not include any activity which is carried on by a person who has been engaged in the business of manufacturing, supplying goods for his own use. It is only when the use is made for the use or for the benefit of the community that is used for the manufacture or sale of goods for its own use and for the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community. [781B C;781A] 4. The definition of "sale" has been given in Entry 49 of List 1, which refers to "any article of food". It means any article of a food which is used or intended to be used for any other purpose. [783C D] 5. The words "other goods" in the entry are not defined as including "any articles of food" and they have been used as such in the course or execution of a works contract. [784G H; 784A B] 6. The term 'sale ' is used to denote all kinds, things including any article which is intended to take place in the execution of any work undertaken by a company. It includes all types, things and things which are capable of being used for a purpose other than that for which it is engaged or intended. [777B C]. 7. The meaning of "any property" in item 52 is not confined to goods which are used as an article of the food. [779C] 8. The dictionary meaning of 'sale is not to be given to the word, but to include all kinds and things including a thing which is capable of having been used for that purpose. It must be understood in its popular sense. [773E F] 9. The expressions "any other goods" have been defined as "any material used or meant for the execution or execution or the execution thereof". [702B C, D] 10. In view of the definition of 'goods ' in Entry 50, List 1 and entry 52 of list I, the High Court was right in holding that the expression "other articles" in Item 52 of the First Schedule to a State Act must be construed as including all kinds which are intended for the carrying on of the business.

The petitioners, who were working as a lessee of the land in question, applied to the State Government for grant of mining lease for the purpose of granting mining leases. The State Government rejected the applications and issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1957 on the ground that the petitioners had not been able to produce any material before the State Govern ment or the authority concerned in respect of the minerals which were used for mining purposes. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification by filing writ petitions in the High Court contending that the impugned notification was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution and that the State Legislature had no power to impose a tax on mineral rights, and that it was not open to the petitioners to challenge the validity. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned notification is violative of Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitu tion. [775G] 2.1 The impugned notifications are in violation of Article 19(1)(g) of Constitution. It is well settled that the power conferred on the State legislature under article 31 is not absolute but it is subject to any restrictions imposed by or under the Act. [774C D] 2:2. The power conferred upon the State government under Article 31 is a discretionary power and cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. It has been held that the exercise of such power is arbitrary and that there can be no violation of Articles 19(5) and 19(6). [776G H; 776A] 2 :3. The validity of these notifications is not challenged in any court on the grounds that the Act does not violate Article 14 or 19(2)(g). It is only when the State has power to levy a tax, it cannot be said that the legislature has no power under article 19(4) to impose such a tax. [764C] 2 2:1 The power of the State to impose any tax on minerals which are used for the mining purposes is not arbitrary or capricious. It can be exercised only in exceptional cases where there is some material before it, and the exercise by the State is arbitrary or mala fide. [754G H] 2.(a) The impugned Notification is violative Of Article 14 and (6) of Article 31. [ 774C E] 2(b) The power to grant mining leases for a period exceeding three years is not subject to restrictions imposed under article 14. [784F G] 3:2 The power given to the Government under section 5(1), read with Rule 4(3) of Gujarat Minor Minerals Concession Rules 1957 is subject only to restrictions which are imposed by the Act and not otherwise. [794C F] 3.(c) The State Legislature has no authority to impose the tax on the minerals used for a mining purpose. It cannot be held that it is arbitrary, irrational or mala fides. [744F H; 771A B] 4:3. There can be two conditions namely (i) that the mineral rights in respect thereof are not subject only of restrictions imposed upon the right to carry on business and (ii) that there is no violation either of Article 301 or Article 19. [734G] 5:4. The first condition is that the lessee shall pay royalty at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per annum from the date of commencement of the Act, and if he fails to pay the royalty within the stipulated period, it will be open to him to challenge such a restriction on the right conferred by Article 19 or Article 31 of the constitution. [724G G] 5.5.

The appellant was a Hindu Religious Trust. The respondent, who was the founder of the temple, filed a suit for declaration that he was the holder of the office of the trustee and that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 4(1) (a) of the Madras Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the office was not an office of trustee but was an office in which the appellant had been appointed as a trustee. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "office" used in section 4 (1) of Madras Hindu religious and charitable Trusts Act means office of trustees and includes office of Trustees. HELD: The word "office ' is defined in section 2(g) of that Act to mean office of a trustee or an office which has been appointed by the trustee for the purpose of carrying out the duties of the trust. It is not correct to say that the word " office" used therein means office which is held by the trustees and is held under the authority of the trustees. [612 D] The expression "post" in section 3(1)(a) means office as a member of the family of the founder or an officer of the Board appointed by him for carrying out his duties as trustee. It does not mean office which can be held by a person who is appointed to perform the functions of the manager. [712 D E] The word 'office" in the context of the expression 'office ' means office and includes offices which are held by him under the control of the Trustee.

The prosecution case was that on the date of occurrence, the deceased and his brother were returning home to the village where he was sitting. The deceased was sleeping in a cot near the house of one P.W. 1. He saw the accused running away from the scene of occurrence. At about 10 p.m., P.Ws. 2 and 3 were standing near the place of occurrence and they saw the dead body of P. W. 1, who was sitting on the cot. The accused persons were seen by the deceased in a room where he saw the deceased lying on the floor. He was also seen by him in a nearby room. At that time P. Ws. 2 & 3 were present at the scene and they were identified by them as eye witnesses. The prosecution case against the accused was that he had seen the accused persons sitting on a cot, while P.w. 1 was standing near his house. He also saw the appellant lying on a floor. The trial court convicted him under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, the High Court confirmed the conviction of the accused under section 201 read with s.34 I. P.C., but reduced the sentence to one year rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of P P. PWs 2 and 4 is not consistent with the prosecution case, because they were interested witnesses in the occurrence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [775 C] 2. The evidence of the eye witnesses is consistent only with the evidence and the evidence on record. It is not possible to accept the testimony of P,Ws. 3 and 4 as they were related to the occurrence, because the deceased was sitting in a position near the cot and he had been seen by them at the time when the accused person came out. The fact that the deceased had seen him at the place where the accused party arrived at the spot would not make any difference. [771 C D] 3. The testimony of PWs 2 & 4 is consistent with their evidence. It has also to be borne in mind that the witnesses were interested in the incident and they are interested witnesses. [762 F G] 4. The eye witnesses who were related by the accused were not related to them. They were not interested witnesses at all. There was no reason why the witnesses should not be related to any of the prosecution witnesses. It was also not possible for the High Courts to accept their testimony as truthful and reliable. [751 C] 5. The conviction of A 1 under section 34 is set aside. The appeal is allowed.

The assessee was the Karta of a Hindu undivided family. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the deceased to tax on his total income and assessed the same to tax under section 10(2) (xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income received by him from the firm was not taxable in view of section 10 (2). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the assessee that the Income tax officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income under section 12(1)(xv) and that the assessment made by him was not correct. HELD : The expression "income" in section 12 (1) (xiv) means income received from a Hindu family. In the present case, the income was received by the firm as his total assets were not taxable. [419 D] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. B. P. Ltd., ; , referred to. The expression 'income" is used in section 10 and it is not necessary that the assessee should have been assessed for the purpose of assessment under section 11(2). The word "income ' in section 13 (1)(xiv) has a wide connotation and includes income received or received by a Hindu, family. [519 D E] Commissioner Of Income tax, Bombay vs M. P., Ltd., , referred only to. In view of the language used in the section it is clear that the expression " income" in the Act means income which is received by an assessee from his father and not as income. The word 'income ' has been used in a wide sense and it cannot be said that the word " income ' in the context of the definition must mean income received, or received from any Hindu family but only as income received. [619 D F] Commissionerof Income tax Bombay vs B.P. Ltd. , referred not to.

The petitioners who were recruited as a direct recruit in the Andhra Pradesh State, challenged the validity of the Andhra Act on the ground that they had no locus standi to challenge the validity. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the impugned Act was not within the competence of Parliament under article 31A(1) (a) and (b). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the provisions of the impugned Acts were ultra vires the Constitution as they contravened articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31(2) and 31(3) of the Constitution. HELD : The impugned Act is not within its competence because it contravenes article 14 of the Constitu tion. It is well settled that the State Legislature has no power to make laws for the purpose of securing the services of persons appointed to a service or post in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State. [419 F G] The impugned Acts are not within their competence and are therefore ultra vires article 31 A(1). [420 H; 820 A B] The State Legislature is competent to make law for the purposes of securing that services of a person appointed to another service or posts in connection therewith are not required by article 31B. It has no authority to make such laws. The impugned provisions do not contravene articles 14 and 19(2). [821 F G; 822 A B]. The impugned sections are ultra vires articles 14 & 19(3). [723 C] The petitioners were appointed as direct recruit on the basis of their qualifications prescribed by the impugned Rules. They were appointed to the service orpost in connection thereto. Their appointment was made on the recommendation of the Public Service Commission and they were not entitled to any protection under article 14. [822 A D].

The appellant was tried for the offence of theft of a house belonging to one Ram Narain, who had been in possession of a stolen house. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 409 I.P.C. and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal by special leave, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had wrongly relied upon the evidence of the witnesses who were in possession and had not taken into account the fact that the appellant had been found in possession. HELD : (i) The High Court was wrong in holding that the evidence led by the prosecution was inadmissible as the witnesses were not examined at the trial, and that the conviction was based on no evidence. [657 H] (ii) The finding of the High court that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles recovered from the appellant were stolen property was erroneous. It is well settled that the presumption under section 5(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, is not available in a case where the evidence has been led by a person who is in possession or has been in actual possession of any stolen house and has failed to discharge his burden of proving that he had taken into custody. The presumption under s.5(1) (a) is not attracted when the facts are established beyond reasonable doubt. [757 H; 758 A] (iii)The High Court erred in holding the appellant guilty of theft. [781 B C] (iv)The finding of fact recorded by the trial court that there was no evidence to show that the article recovered from him was stolen property is erroneous and must be set aside. The High Courts have rightly relied upon it.

The appellants were convicted under section 409 I.P.C., and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed the application on the ground that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to pass an order of transfer, and that the order was not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no power to review its own order under section 115 C.P., and that there was no power in the High court to review the order. HELD : (i) The High Courts have no jurisdiction in the matter, because, the High Courts were not justified in interfering with the order of the Magistrate. [408 D] (ii) In the instant case, the order passed by the High Commis sioner was a nullity and it was not open to the High courts to review their own order. The order was therefore vitiated by error apparent from the face. [416 E F] (iii) The order of this Court is set aside and the matter remanded to the Magistrate for fresh disposal according to law. [414 D] In the present case, there was a clear averment that the complainant had made an application before the High Power Committee under section 151 C. P., and the Magistrate was not justified by his order dated November 5, 1963. The Magistrate had also no jurisdiction under section 116 C.p. The appellants were therefore entitled to review his own order on the grounds of error apparent upon the face and the record produced before him.

The appellant was charged with murder and the evidence of P.W. 1, a police officer who had seen the occurrence, was that he had seen his brother in law to be present at the time when the incident took place. The Sessions Judge convicted him under section 302 I.P.C. but acquitted him on the ground that he was not present at that time and that he did not know the occurrence. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the evidence given by P.Ws. 1 and 2 in their statements recorded under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not sufficient to sustain the conviction of the appellant under section 307 I. P.C., but it is sufficient if they were present at a time when they were seen at the scene of occurrence. The fact that the appellant had seen him at the place of occurrence does not make any difference in the circumstances of the case. The evidence given to the police officer is sufficient to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and it is not necessary for the High Court to have relied on the evidence in order to sustain his conviction under section 201 I. p.C.; Held, further, that there was no reason why the appellant should be convicted under section 34 I. A.I.R. 1960 S.C.) and sentenced him to death. The circumstances of this case are not sufficient for convicting the appellant. The High Court had rightly relied on it. The appellant could not have been convicted under s.302 I.A. in view of the fact that he knew the occurrence at the relevant time when he was seen at a place where the incident taken place and the appellant was present at his scene.

The respondents filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the election of the appellants to the Municipal Council, Jabalpur. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioners had failed to prove their case beyond reasonable doubt and that the notice was not served on them within the time prescribed by Rule 5(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Rules, 1959. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition under article 226 of Constitution inasmuch as the notice in question was served on the petitioners within the period of limitation prescribed by rule 5(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notice in the present case was served upon the petitioners after the expiry of the period prescribed by Rules 5(3) and 5(4) of that Rules. [737C] 2. Rule 5 (2) is a mandatory provision which requires the Collector to serve on the persons concerned, who are interested in the election to fill up the vacancies in accordance with the procedure laid down in Rule 5. The petitioners had not filed any affidavit or evidence in support of their claim. They had also not filed an affidavit or affidavit in support thereof. [781D] 3. In view of the fact that the Collector had served on each of the persons mentioned in the notice, the High court was right in holding that there was no sufficient cause for the delay in filing the petition. [783E F] 4. The writ petitions are dismissed.

The respondent was a company carrying on business in the State of Hyderabad. The company had been prosecuted for an offence under section 420 read with section 34 I.P.C. and section 5(2) (a) of the Companies Act, 1956. The trial court acquitted the respondent but convicted him under section 409 read with sections 109 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to try the case because the charge against the company was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond reasonable doubts that the company had committed an offence. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the charge under section 471 read with s 34 I I. P.C., was not established beyond reasonable time. [757 H] (ii) In view of the provisions of section 5 (2) of that Act, the High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the offence had been committed by a company within the meaning of section 195(1)(b) of Companies Act. [754 B C] (iii) The charge under s.420 read with Section 34 I .P. C., was proved beyond doubt and the prosecution failed to establish beyond reasonable reasonable doubt that the accused had committed the offence. [75 G H] In the present case, the charge was not made out beyond reasonable period of time. It is true that the trial court had found that the charges were proved beyond all reasonable doubt. But in view of section 4(2), it could not be said that the evidence was sufficient to prove the charge beyond reasonable limit. The High Courts have also found that there was no evidence to show that the directors of the company were guilty of an offence punishable under section 467 read with 34 I,P.c.

The respondent was convicted of an offence under section 7(1) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his petition on the ground that the trial had not been concluded within the meaning of article 20(3) of that Constitution and that the State Government had no power to make any order for the trial of an accused person under section 3 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that the High Court had no jurisdiction to make a reference to the High court under article 226 of the Constitution; (ii) that in view of the provisions of article 14 of the Constitu tion, the State Legislature could not have made any order under section 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and that it was not open to the State to make an order for trial of the accused person. HELD : (i ) The High Courts had no inherent power to issue a writ of certiorari to quash the proceedings in respect of offences committed by them under sections 7(2) and 8 of the Indian Penal Code, because they were not competent to issue such a writ. [707 D] (ii). The State Government was not competent in making an order under article 20 of the constitution to make the reference to a High Court under section 5 of the Criminal Procedure Code. It is only when it comes to the conclusion that the case against the accused persons was covered by the provisions Of section 6, that the power conferred on the State Govern ment was not confined to offences committed in respect Of which the State had no authority to make such an order. The State Legislature has no power under article 32 of the Consti tution to make it a law for the purpose of making any law for or in connection with the affairs of the State.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor of Medical Medicine in the Central Government Medical College, Delhi. He was promoted to the post of Professor of Medicine on March 31, 1966. The appellant was selected for appointment as Professor of Surgery on the ground that he had not been appointed as Professor on the basis of his experience in the Institute. The Selection Committee recommended the appellant 's name for promotion to the higher post of Principal of a Medical College. The recommendation of the Selection Committee was accepted by the Central Administrative Tribunal and the appellant was promoted as Professor in Medicine on April 1, 1966 on the grounds that he was not qualified for appointment to the said post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had been appointed to the posts of Professor in Surgery on March 1, 1967 and that his experience as Professor was not a disqualification for promotion under the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appellant ' is entitled to be considered for promotion as Professor from the post held by him on the date of his appointment as Principal of the Medical College in question. [615E] In the instant case, the appellant has been appointed on March 3, 1966 and he was promoted on the post on the same day. The post of Dr. R.K. Jain is a Professor in the Medicine on the recommendation of Selection Committee. He has not been selected for promotion on the said date. [715F] In view of the fact that the post is a Principal of an Medical College and there is no provision in the Rules to make any distinction between the post and the post. [781E F] The appellant had not challenged the appointment of Dr R. K. Jain as Professor by the Medicine, on the other hand, on March 2, 1966, and he has been promoted as a Principal on the footing that he is qualified for promotion in the post from which he was appointed.

The workmen of the appellant company were employed in the manufacture of sugar. The workmen claimed that they were entitled to a minimum wage for the period during which they worked as a result of the strike. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled only to a basic wage for each year and not to a higher wage than what was fixed by the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had erred in holding that the workers were entitled under the provisions of the Act to a maximum wage for every year. The minimum wage fixed by it was only Rs. 10,000/ per month and not Rs. 20,000 per month. [408 B] (ii) The workmen were not entitled to any basic wage as they had worked as an integral part of the industry. They were entitled in the circumstances of the case to a total wage for all the years. Their claim was based on the formula laid down by this Court in Associated Cement Companies Ltd. vs Its Workmen, [1960] 2 S.C.R. 869 and applied. (iii) The minimum wages fixed by this court in Associated cement Company Ltd. were not adequate to meet the demands of the workmen. The basic wage was Rs. 25,000 for each of the years and the workmen had been paid a minimum of Rs. 50,000 as dearness allowance. [414 C D] (iv) The award of the Tribunal is set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal for fresh disposal according to law.

The assessee, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 34(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, calling upon the assessee to show cause why he should not be assessed to tax for that year. The assessee filed his return on March 31, 1961 and claimed that he had no knowledge of the fact that the income was received by him from the firm. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under s 34(2) was issued in respect of the assessment years 1960 61 and 1960 61, but the Income Tax officer did not accept the explanation offered by the assessee. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notice under sub section (1) is a notice under the Act and it is only when the income is received by the firm that he has received it from the partnership firm that the Income tax Officer has no jurisdiction to issue the notice. [657 D] (ii) The notices issued under section 148 of the Act are not in respect Of the assessment for the year 1960 62, but they relate to the assessment of income for the years 1960 63 and 1960 62. The notice is a mere formality and does not require any further proof that the assessee has received the amount from the partners. [757 D E] (iii) The Income tax officer has no power to issue a notice in respect thereof under section 147 of the Income Act, 1961. The notices are not intended to be issued by the Income. Tax Officer for the purpose of issuing the notice and it cannot be said that the notices were issued without any further evidence.

The appellant firm was carrying on business in the Indian State of Madras. The Income tax Officer held that the partnership was not a registered firm and therefore, the income from the business could be taxed under section 10(2) (xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment but the High Court in reference held that there was no question of any change in the constitution of the firm and that the appellant had not been a registered partnership firm. The High Court answered the question in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the word "business" in section 10 (2) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1961 means any business which is carried on by a person who has been appointed as such under the provisions of the Act and not by the person who is appointed as an agent of the partnership. HELD: The word "office" in the section includes a person whose principal place of business is carried upon by a partner or a partner, but does not include a person holding any office in the firm. It is only when the business is done by a member of the family that he has been so appointed and that he cannot be said to have been appointed under the Act. [657 H] The word 'business" means an activity which is carrying on by him as such, but not as a partner. In the present case, the appellant was a registered dealer and it was only when he was appointed under section 12(2)(xv) that he had been appointed in the partnership firm, that he was not liable to be taxed because he was holding any other office in that firm. [757 H; 758 A] The High Courts were right in holding that the business of the partners was a separate and distinct entity and that it was not an activity carried on under the Indian Companies Act. The question whether the appellant could be assessed to income tax under section 11(2).

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the adopted son of one G and his wife. The respondent, who was the sole surviving coparcener in the suit, filed a suit for partition of the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff had no right to the property as he had not been the adopted daughter of G and her husband. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in law in holding that there was a valid partition between G and the wife and the defendant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding the plaintiff 's suit as he was adopted son by G and not by G. [408 D] In the instant case, the plaintiff was adopted daughter by G on the basis of a valid gift deed dated March 31, 1960. The plaintiff had been adopted son in the partition of his joint family property. The adoption deed did not mention that the defendant had adopted son 's wife and her children were adopted son. [508 D E] In view of the provisions of section 4(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the widow was entitled to the share of G on partition. [511 C] The High Courts erred in holding in favour of the plaintiff. [608 F] The question whether the adoption deed dated April 31, 1961 was valid or not is a question of law and must be decided by the High Courts.

The respondent Corporation, a public limited company, was incorporated in the United Provinces and Berar State Road Transport Corporation. The employees of the Corporation were governed by the provisions of the , as amended from time to time. The Corporation took over the management of the corporation under section 10(2) of the Act. The respondent Corporation terminated the services of the employees on the ground that they had been appointed in a temporary capacity and had not been confirmed in service, and that the Corporation was not competent to terminate the services. The appellant Corporation filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the termination order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the termination of service of the employee was illegal and void as it was not made by the Corporation under section 12(2)(b) of , and that no such action could be taken against him in respect of his services. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 12 (2)(a) of Act are not intended to confer any power on the Corporation to terminate a service of an employee who has been appointed as a temporary employee. It is only when the Corporation has taken over the administration of the company that it was competent to continue in service and that it could not be said that the employees had been confirmed or confirmed in the service, it would be open to the Corporation either to terminate his services or to terminate such service. [742C] 2. The terms of section 10 (2) are clear and unambiguous and they do not require any express provision for the termination by the employee. The object of the section is to provide for the continuance of an existing employee in a permanent capacity, and to provide that the employee should be deemed to have been confirmed on the date he was appointed in that capacity. [771C] 3. The power conferred upon the Corporation by section 12 is not confined to the appointment of a temporary servant in a substantive capacity or in a post in which he has been employed. It does not contemplate any such appointment, but only when it provides for an employee to be confirmed in that service. The expression 'appointing authority ' means the appointing authority who is appointed by the appointing authori ty under section 3(2). [774C] 4. The word 'appoint ing authority ' has been defined in section 2(g) of that Act as meaning a person who is employed for a period not exceeding six months or more, and it does not mean that he has continued in service on the appointed day. [764F G] 5. The term 'appoint ment ' means a person appointed to a temporary post in connection with the affairs of the State. The words 'appoint ed by the word ' appointing authority ' are wide enough to include a person holding a permanent post in the same capacity as an employee in the former or in the latter or in another, and the expression ' appointing Authority ' means any person appointed by it under section 16(2), but not a person employed in connection therewith. The definition of 'appointa tive authority ' is wide enough. It has been used in the context of the term ' appointing authoris ty '. The expressions 'appointi ty ' and 'appointee ' are defined in the Act to mean a person on the appointment or promotion of a permanent employee in connectionwith his affairs, whether permanent or temporary, and not any person who was appointed by him under section 17(2); and the word "appointing Authority" is wide. The meaning of the expression "appoint ing Authority ' is that the appointing Authority has been constituted for a limited period of six months and not for a term exceeding six years.

The appellants were members of the Bar Council of Punjab. They were members in the Bar Association of the Punjab. The Bar Council was to be constituted by the Governor for the purpose of carrying out the functions and duties of the Court. The appellants were also members of a Bar Council. The Chief Justice of India, however, did not accept the suggestion that the Chief Justice had no power to act as a Judge of the High Court. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to act under article 136 of the Constitution and that the appellants were entitled to be represented by their counsel. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court has not acted in any manner whatsoever with the aid of the Chief Judge. [775F] 2. The order of the Single Judge is set aside and the matter remanded to the Chief Judicial Magistrate for disposal according to law. [771C D] 3. The learned Single Judge should dispose of the matter afresh after giving an opportunity to the appellants to show cause why he should not be represented. [762F] 4. The appeal must accordingly be allowed. The judgment and order of this Court are set aside. The contempt petition is restored to its original file. [751G] 5. The Registry shall send a copy of this order to the learned Single judge for information. [781C E] 6. The matter should be placed before the Chief Secretary for information and on receipt of such intimation, the Chief Minister shall take necessary steps to see that the case is disposed of expeditiously.

The petitioner company was a public limited company carrying on business in the Indian State. The Income tax Officer issued notices under section 34(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922 to show cause why penalty should not be imposed upon them for failure to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for the purpose of investigation. The petitioners filed their objections to the notice. The petitioner contended that the notices were invalid as they had been issued without complying with the provisions of section 34 (1) and (2) of that Act and that the proceedings under section 5(4) of Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1948 were not barred by limitation. Held, that the provisions Of section 5 (4) and 5 (5) of this Act are mandatory and must be read together as they are directory and not mandatory. The words "any person aggrieved by an order of assessment" in section 5 of the Act mean a person aggrieved against an order made under section 4(1). The words 'any person affected by an orders of assessment ' means any person aggrieved thereby, whether before or after the commencement of the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act. The word "any other person aggrieved" in the context of the provisions contained in section 6(4), are wide enough to include a person who is aggrieved by such order. The expression "any persons affected by the orders of the assessment ' includes any person affected thereby, and any person interested in an order under section 6 (4), may be affected by such orders as may be made by the Income Tax Officer before the commencement Of the Constitution. The provisions of sections 5(1)(a) and 6(3) are mandatory. It is not necessary that a person affected must be given an opportunity to show his case against the order of the income tax officer. The object of the section is to prevent abuse of the process of the court, and to secure the ends of justice. The purpose of the sections is to protect the interests of the public and to prevent evasion of tax. It has been found that the Act was passed in contravention of the principles of natural justice. It was not necessary for a person to show that he had been affected by any order made by him under section 3(1), but that he should be given opportunity to explain his case. The Act is therefore ultra vires and void as it contravened article 14 of the Constitu tion.

The Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd. was incorporated in the Delhi Cloth & General Mills (Regulation of Employment) Act, 1958. The Delhi Cloth Mills Ltd., was incorporated under the Delhi General Clauses Act, 1957. The appellant company was carrying on business as a dealer in the manufacture of cloth and cloth. It was registered as a firm under the . The appellant was prosecuted for contravention of section 2(1)(d) of the . On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the appellant was not a "dealer" within the meaning of section 3(2)(d). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the definition of "business" in section 2 (1)(e) of Act, includes any activity which is carried on by or on behalf or for the benefit of the general public. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The definition of 'business" is wide enough to include a business which is engaged in the carrying on of the business of the company and it is not necessary that the activity should be carried on with the aid of the community. [630 H] In the instant case, the appellant had been carrying on the business as an agent of the respondent company. The respondent was not carrying on any business for the purpose of carrying on its business. It is not disputed that the respondent was a "business". The definition does not include any activity carried on in or on the behalf of a general public but it is only a business carried on. [730 H; 730 A] In view of the definition, the expression 'business ' includes any business which has been carried on for the purposes of carrying out its business and cannot be said to be an activity carried by or for any other purpose. The definition is wide in terms and it does not mean that the activities carried on are carried on without the aid or aid of a particular community. It does not contemplate any activity as a "industry" within section 2.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family. The income tax authorities assessed the income of the assessee on the basis that the income from the land was not taxable under section 4(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the amount of compensation payable to the assessee was not liable to be included in his total income. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the expression "income" in section 4 (1)(b) of that Act includes income from land and that the word "income ' in section 5(1) (a) means income from property which is held by a person who has been appointed as an agent or trustee. HELD : The High Courts were right in holding that the assessee had not been assessed to income tax under section 6 of the Act. [408 D] In the present case, the income was not assessable under section 5 (1) of 1922. It was not disputed that the land which was held by him as an individual and was not a joint family property. The question whether the income received by the assessee from the lands was taxable under the Act is not one of fact. [508 D F] In view of the definition in section 2(a) (i) of this Act, it must be held that income received from the assessee could not be included for purposes of the income tax. The expression " income" in the context of the word 'income ' is used in the sense in which it occurs. It means income received or received by a Hindu person as an independent source and includes income received therefrom. [511 D] Commissioner of Income tax, Bihar vs Srikakulam Municipality, ; , referred to.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Director of Factories in the year 1981. They were promoted to the post of Assistant Director on ad hoc basis and they were promoted as Assistant Directors on ad temporary basis. The respondents challenged the promotion order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants are entitled to be considered for promotion to the posts of Assistant Directors in the establishment of the Factories. They are entitled only to be promoted as Deputy Director on regular basis and not on ad permanent basis. [775G] 2.2 The appellants have been appointed as Deputy Directors on temporary basis and their seniority has been fixed at Rs.4,000 per month. Their seniority is determined in accordance with the rules framed by the Government of India under Rule 3(a) of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1965. [771G] 3.3 The appellants were promoted on ad interim basis and the respondents are entitled for their promotion as Deputy Superintendent on ad regular basis. They have been given seniority at Rs.,4,500 per month in accordance to the rules. Their promotions are not being disturbed by the Court of law. [762C D] 4.4 In view of the fact that the appellants were initially appointed as Senior Assistant on ad ad hoc promotion, they cannot be said to have been promoted as Senior Assistants on ad officiating basis and that their seniority was determined in terms of the rules made under Rule 2(a). [773G H; 771A] 5.4 The respondents are directed to consider the case of the appellants for promotion as Senior Clerk on ad basis with effect from 1st April, 1982 within a period of three months from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this order. [783C D].

The Karnataka Motor Vehicles (Regulation of Transport and Transport) Act, 1984 was enacted to provide for the grant of permits to persons who are not registered under the Act. Section 68(1)(b) provides that no permit shall be granted except in accordance with the provisions of section 68(2). The State Government issued a notification dated March 1, 1985, providing inter alia for the transport of motor vehicles and for the carriage of motor vehicle. The appellants who were registered under section 68 (1)(a) applied to the Regional Transport Authority for grant of permit on the ground that they had not been registered under any Act. The Regional Transport Authorities rejected their applications. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal held that the Regional transport Authority was not competent to grant permits in accordance therewith and that the State Government had no power to grant a permit in accordancewith the provisions contained in section 68. The High Court, however, allowed the writ petitions holding that the notification dated April 1, 1984 did not apply to the appellants who had been registered as a "State Transport Undertaking" under the Karnataka Motor Vehicle (Regulation and Transport and Amendment) Act 1984. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the expression "State transport undertaking" in section 2(b) of the Act includes the State Transport Undertaking, and that it is not necessary to give a restricted meaning to the word "State" in the proviso to section 68 of the Karnataka Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word " State Transport Corporation" in sub section (1) of section 2 of the Mysore Act means the State transport undertaking which is registered under an Act and not under any other law for the time being in force. [794E] 2. The expression " State transport Undertaking" in clause (b) includes the Central Government, and the Regional Regional Transport authority has to be given a restricted interpretation to the words "State Government". The word 'State ' is used in the context of the definition of "State ' in section 3(b). [795E] 3. The words " State Government" in clauses (a) to (e) are not intended to include the Central Transport Undertaking as a whole and not merely the State of Karnataka. [771F G] 4. The proviso to sub section(1) is intended to cover all persons who have been registered or registered under a Act. It is clear from the language used in sub sections (1), (2) and (3) that the word ' State ' has been used in contradistinction to the expression 'State Transport undertaking '. [764F G; 771A B] 5. The object of the proviso is to provide inter alia the transport services, including the transport facilities, for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the said Act and to provide a uniform scheme for the nationalisation of motor transport vehicles and to make it available to persons registered under that Act. [754F H; 772A B].

The respondent was a dealer in the State of Madras. The respondent sold certain goods to the appellant on July 1, 1948. The Sales Tax Officer issued notices under section 3(1) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 for recovery of tax due from him. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notices and the High court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sales were not liable to be taxed under section 4(1)(a) of that Act as the respondent had failed to pay tax within the time prescribed by r. 3(2). HELD : The Sales tax Officer was competent to assess the tax due and payable by him under the Act. [408 C] The High Court was right in holding that the respondent was liable to pay sales tax on the sale of goods for the purpose of assessment of tax under section 5(1). The High court was wrong in holding the sales to be taxable under section 6(1), and that the Sales Tax officer was competent under r. 4(2) to assess tax due under section 7(1); and that, therefore, the respondent could not be taxed as a dealer under section 8(1 ) (a). [409 C] In the present case, the sales effected by the respondent were liable to tax under the Madras Act. The sales were made in the course of inter State trade or commerce within the meaning of section 2(2)(a). The SalesTax Officer was not competent to make a demand for the recovery of the tax payable under the provisions of the Act and that therefore, he could not have been taxed as an dealer under the Tamil Nadu General Sales tax Act.

The appellant was a member of the Indian State and was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct. The respondent filed an appeal against the order of dismissal passed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad, which was allowed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the order was not in accordance with law and was therefore illegal as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution. HELD : (i) The order of the High court was not a decree within the meaning of article 136 of the Consti tution, because the High Courts had no jurisdiction to pass an order of discharge under section 7(1)(b) of the Act. [775 G] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was guilty of professional misconduct and not of professional conduct. [774 D E] (iii) The appellant was entitled to a decree for arrears of salary, allowances and other benefits under section 8(1) (b). The order was therefore not a judgment within the scope of article 134. [764 G H; 775 A B] (iv) The decree passed by this Court in appeal against that order is not a final decree within article 136. [784 D F] (v) The question whether the appellant had been dismissed from services under section 3(1), (b) or (c) of , does not arise for consideration in this case. [754 G] In the present case, the appellant did not pay any salary to him as he was a probationer and was not paid any salary. The High Courts were right in taking the view that the respondent had been denied the benefit of section 7 (1)(a) of . [775 D E].

The appellant, a lessee of the land in dispute, was granted lease to the respondents for mining coal. The respondents were granted lease on the ground that they had no right to use the land for any purpose whatsoever. The appellants filed a suit against the respondents claiming compensation for the period from April 1, 1943 to March 31, 1944. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the respondents had not proved that they were in possession of the lands and that the lease was for a period of more than six years. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the appellants had failed to prove that they are in possession thereof. Held, that the suit was barred by limitation under article 136 of the Constitution. The suit was not barred by time as the respondents were in actual possession of their lands and therefore the suit could not be decreed on the basis of the pleadings of the parties. The High Court erred in reversing the findings of the trial court and dismissing the suit. Held further, that there is no presumption under section 4(1) of the Bihar Land Revenue Code that a lessee has no right or title to the land. The appellant had not established that they have been in possession for more than three years. The question whether the respondents are in actual physical possession of any land is essentially one of fact and it cannot be said that they did not prove that the land was in possession. Held also, further,that the suit must fail by reason of the provisions of section 4 (1) (a) of Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The plea of limitation under section 5(1)(b) of Act is a mixed question of law and fact and the courts below have rightly held that they failed to establish that they was in actual occupation for more years.

The appellant was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from services under r. 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Rules, 1958. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal and also for quashing the order. The High Court held that the termination of the appellant was illegal as it amounted to misconduct within the meaning of section 2(s) of that Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of discharge passed by the Industrial Tribunal is not a punishment but an order of punishment and does not amount to punishment. [619 F] (ii) The appellant was not entitled to any relief under r, 7(2). The order did not contain any provision for the dismissal of the employee on the grounds that it amounted only to misconduct. The order was therefore illegal as the order was passed without giving him a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action. [719 F G] (iii) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order under r., 7(3). The appellant could not be dismissed from his service because it did not give any reasons for its dismissal. [779 H; 742 A B] (iv) The High Courts were right in holding that the order passed by a Industrial Tribunal was illegal and the order made by the Tribunal was not justified. The Tribunal was therefore right in quashing the orders of dismissal. The appeal must be dismissed.

The appellants, who were lessees of a cinema theatre, filed a suit for possession of the cinema theatre on the ground that they had been in lawful occupation of the said cinema theatre. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the lease was not a lease and that the defendants were entitled to possession of it under section 3(1) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High Court held that the agreement between the parties was void as it had been entered into by the parties with the consent of the parties and that there was no agreement between them and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that a lease was a lease within the meaning of section 3 (1) of that Act and not a contract for the sale of cinema theatre and that it was not an agreement for the transfer of the licence. [637 D] (ii) The suit was not maintainable because the defendants had entered into a compromise with the parties, but had been given a right to possession thereof under section 13(1)(a) read with section 13 of the Act. [738 G H] (iii) The trial Court was right in dismissing the suit on the grounds that the plaintiffs were entitled only to possession and not for the purpose of the lease. [783 D F] (iv) The defendants had failed to prove that they were in lawful possession of cinema theatres. They had also failed to establish that they acted in lawful faith or in breach of their contract.

The respondent was appointed as a temporary Assistant in the State of Uttar Pradesh on 1.1.1986 and he was confirmed in service on 30.9.1988. The respondent was working as a Deputy Superintendent in the Government of India. He was appointed to officiate in the post of Deputy Superintendent on 30th September, 1986. On 30th October, 1985 he was appointed on 30st September, 1985. In the meantime, he was absorbed in the U.P. State Civil Service (Executive Branch) and was confirmed as a permanent Assistant in that State. He continued to hold the post till 30th November, 1985 when he was working in the said State. The State Government issued an order dated 1st October, 1986 directing the respondent to continue in service until 30th April, 1985 and on his failure to do so, he filed a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the petition holding that the respondent was entitled to be absorbed in U. P. State. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that since he had been appointed as Deputy Superintendent, he could not be treated as permanent Assistant on 30 th September, 1984 and his services were terminated without notice to him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding: (1) that the order of termination was illegal and void; (2) that since the respondent had been working in UP State, he would have been entitled to continue to hold his post till 31st October 1985 when his services had been terminated on 30rd September, 1987. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of appointment dated 30th August, 1986 was illegal as it was not made applicable to the respondent since he was in service after 30th June, 1985; (3) that he was entitled only to continue as Deputy Superintendents on 30 st October, 1984 when he had already been appointed on 29th September. 1985 and his service was terminated on 31st March, 1985 by giving him a notice of termination of his services without assigning any reason. [730F] 2. The appellant was appointed in the year 1982 and he continued to be in service till 30 th November, 1984. He had been confirmed as Deputy Collector on 30nd October, 1988 when he joined the State Civil Services (Executive) and he had not completed the period of probation for a period of two years. His services were regularised by giving effect to the order dated 31st December, 1986 and his appointment was terminated in accordance with the order passed by the High court. The period of service rendered by him during the period from 1st April, 1984 to 30th March, 1984 was not counted as permanent service. [777F] 3. The services of the respondent were regularised on 30/9th September 1985 and he could be deemed to have been confirmed in that post till the date of his appointment. He did not join the State Government till 30st October 1984 when his service had been regularised. His service was regularised by the State Govern ment on 30 1st November, 1986 when he continued in service. The re spondents were entitled to get the benefit of the order. [781G] 4. The appointment of respondent as Deputy Secretary on 29.9th October 1985 was not valid because he had completed the probationary period of three years. He could not have been appointed to the State Police till 30.10.1984 when he attained the age of 58 years. The fact that he had joined the Government service after 31st July, 1984 would not make him a permanent employee. [783G] 5. The petitioner was entitled for the benefit under the order and his salary was fixed at Rs.4,000 per month. He should have been paid the salary as per the order in question.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellant on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in the murder case, and that the evidence of P.W. 1, who was a witness to the occurrence, was not corroborated by any other evidence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court erred in interfering with the order of acquittal passed by the Sessions Judge on the basis of the evidence adduced by the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court has rightly held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that there was no sufficient ground for interference with the judgment of acquittal. [775G] (2) In the instant case, the High court erred in not interfering with an order of conviction passed by a Sessions Judge. [771C D] (3) The evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not consistent with the innocence of the accused and that they were falsely implicated. They were not examined at the trial. The evidence was not sufficient to sustain the conviction. [761G] In the present case, there was nothing on record to show that the appellant had been convicted for the murder of P or about the deceased. The prosecution witnesses did not support the prosecution case and the High Courts erred in holding that the acquittal of the appellants was justified. [753E F] (4) The fact that the accused had been acquitted by the trial court, does not make any difference to the sentence imposed on him.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Administrative Service. He was appointed as a Judge of the High Court under section 5(1) (a) read with section 7(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant was charged with offences under sections 161 and 165 IPC read with Section 5(3) of that Act. The trial court convicted him under Sections 161 and 164 IPC but acquitted him on the ground that he had been in possession of a public servant and that he was not in any way concerned with the affairs of the Union or of the State. On appeal, the High Judge held that the appellant was not a member within the meaning of section 5 (1) readwith Section 7(3). The High Court also held that since the appellant had been holding a public office and was not holding a post in the service of the Government he could not be prosecuted for an offence under section 161 IPC. On further appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression "public servant" is defined in Section 2(c) to mean any person who is or has been in any manner concerned with any public servant. It includes a person who has been holding the post of a Judge or a member thereof and includes a member who has held such office. [710B] 1.2 The expression 'public servant ' means any person, who is, or has held any office in the Government of India or a State. Section 5 (3) provides that no public servant shall be deemed to have been in the employment of any Government servant except with the previous sanction of the Central Government. [771C] 1:3 The expression `public servant " means any member of a service or of any other person who, at the time of his appointment as such, is or was not, in the course of his duties, been in charge of, and has been, in relation to, the affairs or affairs of a State, an officer or servant of a Government. The expression used in Section 5 of the Act means any officer or employee of a Central Government who is in the employ of a Union or a Union Territory. [761C D] 1.(a) In the instant case, the appellant has been working as a member under the State Government and was holding a permanent post in that service. He had been appointed as an Additional Judge in the year 1948. He continued to hold the post in question till he attained the age of superannuation. He could not have been appointed by the Central Govern ment on the basis of his tenure as such. The High Courts were, therefore, right in holding that the order of appointment was illegal and void. [751G] (b) In view of the fact that the charge sheet was filed against him under Section 5 read with Sections 161, 165 and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, it cannot be said that he has been appointed to hold a post under the Government. It is not disputed that the appointment of an Additional judge in the High Courts is illegal or void because the appellant is holding a temporary post under Government. Therefore, the order passed by the High court is liable to be quashed. [781C E] 1(c). The question whether the appellant can be prosecuted under Section 161 IPC is a question of fact and not one of fact. [791F G] (d) In any event, the question whether he was in possession or not is a matter of fact is a mixed question of law and fact. It cannot be disputed that he is holding an office in a Government service or a state. The question as to whether he has held a permanent office under Government is a questions of fact which can be determined by the Supreme Court.

The appellant was elected to the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the West Tripura State. The respondent challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he had been declared elected as a member of the Scheduled Castes and that he was not entitled to be declared elected. The High Court held that the appellant was not qualified to be chosen as a candidate for election to the Bihar Legislative Assembly. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the word "Scheduled Caste" in article 341(1) (a) means a caste which is used as a Scheduled Tribe and that the expression "Scheduled Castes" in the article includes a caste, and that it must be read in its ordinary sense and not in its popular sense. HELD: The word " Scheduled Caste" has been defined in the Constitution to mean a caste or tribe which is intended to be used as an integral part of the community. It is well settled that the words "Scheduled Tribe" are wide enough to include a caste. In the present case, the appellant had not been declared as a scheduled caste. The word ' Scheduled Caste ' has been used in the context of the expression 'Scheduled Castes ' and it must mean a tribe which was intended to have a common object.
