[657 F G] The word `Scheduled Tribe ' is defined in article 342(1)(a) and it is not necessary that a caste should be treated as an scheduled caste, because it has been held by the High Court that the respondent was not a member for election as a result of which he had become a member.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The appellant was in occupation of a flat in Bombay and was in possession of the flat. He was convicted under section 5(1)(a) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial Magistrate acquitted the appellant but the High Court confirmed the conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had committed an offence under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and that he was not a tenant within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. HELD: (i) The word "tenant" in section 5 means a person who is in occupation or has been in possession or has become a tenant for the time being, but does not include a person whose tenancy has been terminated by the landlord and that the words "any person" in the section are wide enough to cover a person against whom an offence is committed. The word 'tenant" is used in the context of the definition of a person as defined in section 2(1) of that Act. It means a tenant who is not in occupation, but only a person in possession and has become an occupant for the purpose of the section. [608 D] (ii) In the present case the appellant was not in actual possession of any flat. The fact that he had been in occupation and has been convicted under sections 161 and 165 of the Penal Code does not make him a tenant liable to be evicted. [709 G H; 709 A B] (iii)The word "landlord" is wide enough, but it means a landlord who is a tenant. The definition of person as given in section 3(1), therefore, includes a person for the purposes of the , and does not mean a person to whom an act is done or is done by him.

The appellant company was a registered firm carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling houses in Bombay. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant company had not been able to pay the dearness allowance for the period between 1st April, 1973 and 31st March, 1977. The Tribunal also found that the dearness allowances were not available to the employees of the appellant Company. The appellant company appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the workmen that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the basic wage structure of the employees was not a fixed wage structure and that the additional dearness allowance should be taken into account while fixing the dearness Allowance for the year 1976 78, and that since the appellant had been able only to pay dearness allowance at the rate of Rs. 10 per month, it could not be said that the increase in the dearness rates was justified by the Tribunal 's award. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The basic wage fixed by the Industrial Tribunal is the minimum wage structure for the employees and the additional Dearness Allowance should be given to the workmen who are employed in the industry. [1090E] 2. The additional dearness allowances of the workers in the appellant 's case were not the same as the basic pay structure of their employees. The dearness allowance was not the higher wage structure which was fixed by it. The minimum wage fixed for the workmen in the company was Rs. 5 per month. The increase in dearness allowance is the same. [1190E F] 3. The award of the Tribunal shows that the increased dearness allowance of the company had been reduced to Rs. 20 per month and the appellant was entitled to the additional allowance at that rate. The High Court has not given any reasons for its conclusion. It is true that the Industrial Court has taken into consideration the increase of dearness allowance in the case of the respondent company, but it does not mean that the change in the basic structure of its employees would be justified by fixing the basic wages of the employee. But the Tribunal has not considered this factor as a matter of fact. [1290E G] 4. The special allowance of Rs 10 per day is not a uniform wage structure. It cannot be said to have been reduced by the award of this Court in the present case. [1391F] 5. The main question for consideration is whether the additional gratuity payable to the appellant should be reduced by a fixed rate or by a higher rate or otherwise, and if so, what is the basic dearness allowance which was given to it. [1490E H; 1090A B] 6. The respondent company has not challenged the award on the ground that the new dearness allowance had been increased by the order of this court in the appeal. It has also not challenged that order.

The appellant, a private limited company, was employed as an Assistant Manager in the respondent Mills. The dispute between the parties related to the payment of wages for the period during which the appellant was paid wages. The appellant claimed that the respondents were entitled to the benefit of section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and that the award was bad because it had been made under section 10(2)(b) of that Act. The respondent contended that the appellant 's claim was not maintainable as the appellant had not paid wages for a period during the period of his employment. Held, that the dispute between them related to payment of salary for the periods during which they were paid and the award made under the Act was bad in law because it was made under an agreement between the appellant and the respondents. The award was therefore valid. The respondents had not been able to prove that the workmen were entitled under section 2 (s) to be paid wages during the relevant period. The question whether the appellant is entitled to any relief under section 3(s), does not arise in this case. The reference made by the appellant to the Industrial Tribunal was not a dispute within the meaning of section 10 (2)(a). The award did not contain any provision for the payment or payment of any wages during that period. It was not open to the appellant, to raise the question as to whether the workmen are entitled under the provisions of the Act. Held further, that in view of the provisions contained in section 2 of the , the dispute relating to payment or wages during a period of employment must be deemed to have been an industrial dispute within section 10 of the . The award made by it was not valid and therefore could not be sustained.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 409, 467 and 471 I.P.C., read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, for having committed an offence punishable under section 409, I. P.C. The prosecution case was that he had been in charge of a public servant and had been responsible to the Government for the conduct of his business. The appellant was convicted by the Magistrate on the ground that he was not guilty of any offence under section 477A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him on the grounds (i) that the sanction given by the Government was not a sanction within the meaning of section 197(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code; (ii) that there was no sanction in respect of the appellant 's conduct and the sanction was not necessary for the prosecution of the respondent. Held, that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant was guilty of an offence under sections 477A and 477A, I, P. C., and (iii) that sanction was a valid sanction within section 197. The sanction given in respect thereof was not one of the conditions precedent for the exercise of the power conferred on it by section 197 of the Cr. P., and the appellant could not be convicted under section 471, I .P. C. The question whether sanction was necessary for prosecution of an accused person is a matter which must be determined by the Court in its discretion. Held further, that sanction given to the appellant under section 197 was not valid as it was not in respect Of the appellant who had been charged with the offence under the Indian Criminal Procedure and was therefore not competent to take cognizance of the offence.

The assessee was a firm carrying on business in the State of Travancore Cochin. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee to tax under section 10(2) (xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and assessed the loss to the extent of Rs. 1,000/ . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the loss was not a trading loss but a trading profit. On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that in view of the provisions of section 10 (2), (xv), the loss could be carried forward only if it had been carried forward for the purpose of carrying on the business of the State and not when the profits were carried forward. The High Court also held that there was no provision in the Act to make a distinction between the profits and gains of the business carried forward by the firm and the profits, therefore, could be set off against the profits of the firm. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that the expression "any loss" in section 10 of the Act must mean only such loss as is carried forward in the course of inter State trade or commerce and not in the manner prescribed by the statute; (ii) that in the present case, the loss suffered by the company was a trading income and therefore, the losses were not carried forward to the assessee. HELD: The High Courts had rightly held that it was a business loss within the meaning of section 2(xv). [637 B C] (2) The expression "other loss" used in section 2 (xv)(xv) means any loss which is carried on by the State or the State, but does not include any loss arising from such business. It is well settled that a loss must be carried out by the carrying on of the trade or business and it must be set up as a trading asset within the definition of "any asset" in the section. [638 C D] (3) The word "other liability" in sub section (1) of section 5 of the Income tax law means a loss which has been carried on in the carrying out of the carrying of the same business or profession and not a loss arising therefrom. It does not mean that the word "any other liability" is used in the context of the expression 'other liability". [639 C D; 635 A] (4) The words "other than an asset" are used in sub sections (1), (2A) and (3). The words used in cl. (xv ) of section 6 of the Incometax Act, 1961, mean a loss incurred by the business or vocation carried on under the carrying or the business.

The respondent company was a registered firm carrying on business in the appellant 's factory. The respondent company had its registered office at Bombay and it was established that the respondent company has been able to discharge its duties as an employee of the appellant company. The Industrial Tribunal held that the age of superannuation for the purpose of gratuity was not fixed by the Industrial Tribunal, but the Tribunal did not agree with the Tribunal that the retirement age of the respondent was not determined by the Tribunal and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the company that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to award any compensation in respect of the employees of the Company and that the award was bad as it was based on a wrong appreciation of evidence and that it was not open to the Tribunal to interfere with the award. HELD : (i) The Tribunal has not given any reasons for its award. It is well settled that the Industrial Tribunals are entitled to award compensation in accordance with the principles laid down by this Court in Associated Cement Companies Ltd. vs Their Workmen, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, followed. (ii) The award of the Tribunal is not based on any wrong appreciation or misdirection. It has been based on no evidence and it cannot be said that there was a mistake in the award which could have been corrected by the High Court. [868 C] (iii) The Industrial Tribunals have no jurisdiction under section 33C(2) of the , to interfere in the matter of retirement age. The Tribunal is entitled to exercise its discretion in accordance only when it finds that there has been a mistake or error apparent on the face of the record.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. The company was carrying on business in the manufacture of certain goods and it was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. It was alleged that the company had been acting as its managing agents for the purpose of carrying on the business in India and that the Company had acted in contravention of section 5(1) (a) of the Act, and that there was no violation of any provisions of the Companies Rules. The Company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Board of Directors dated December 7, 1965, and the order was quashed by the High court on the ground that it had acted under section 5 (1) of that Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Board of directors was not competent to make a general order under section 6(1)(a) or section 5 of the , as the case may be, and therefore the order passed by the Board was invalid. [419 D] (ii) The power conferred on the Central Government under section 4(1), read with section 5, is not confined to the power of the Central Board to make general orders under section 7(1). It is only when it is made by a general or special order that the power conferred by section 6 (1)(b) or sub section (2) of section 7 is subject to the control of the Government. [519 E] (iii) The powers conferred on Central Board under section 8 are not confined merely to the powers of the State Board but also to the functions of the company. It is not necessary that the powers conferred by sections 4(3) and 5 should be exercised in a particular manner. The power of making general orders is limited only to the duties of the officers and servants of the Company. [619 E G] (iv) The Central Board has no power to make any general order, under section 3(1); it is not open to the Central Boards to make such general or specific orders as are necessary for carrying on of the business.

The appellants were charged with offences under sections 302 and 201 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night between 9th and 10th November, 1962, the appellants along with others armed with deadly weapons attacked the deceased and his companions and caused injuries to him. The defence version was that the appellants were not present at the time when the incident took place. The trial court convicted the appellants under section 302 read with s.34 of the Penal Code but acquitted them. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the prosecution case must be accepted. The evidence of the eye witnesses is consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and it is not necessary to prove that they were present at that time when they were seen in the house of the appellants. The circumstances which are peculiar to the case show that the accused had been seen in their house at the relevant time when he was seen in his house at about 10 p.m. The fact that the deceased was seen at the scene of occurrence is not sufficient to prove the guilt. The circumstance that the appellant was seen near the scene and the appellants had been found in their possession at the place where the incident occurred. The circumstantial evidence must be consistent only from the hypothesis but it is a chain of evidence which has to be established beyond reasonable doubt. In the present case, the circumstances proved by the prosecution are not sufficient for the conclusion that the crime was committed with the object of causing death or grievous hurt to the accused.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of medicines under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the said Rules on the ground that they contravened articles 14(1)(g) and (g) of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the impugned Rules violated articles 14 and 19(1) of Schedule I to the Constitution inasmuch as it was not made applicable to the State of Delhi, since the Act did not provide for any restriction on the fundamental right guaranteed under article 19(2) of that Article. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned Rules are ultra vires Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitu tion. [730F] 2.1 The petitioners were manufacturers in medicines under articles 14, 19(3)(g), (g), and (h) of Part III of the Schedule to the Act. They had no right to carry on their trade or business. They were not entitled to carry out any trade or trade in the country. [779F] 3.2 The impugned rules are ultravires tively and cannot be sustained under article 14 of the Consti tution. [777G] 4.3 The petitioners have failed to establish that they were manufacturers within the meaning of articles 14 & 19(4) of Constitution. They have not established that they had been selling medicines in their own name or in any manner whatsoever. They are also entitled to the protection under article 21 of Constitu tion and they are also liable to be punished for breach of any law which is in force at the time of the impugned Act. [781G] 5.4 The petitioners, therefore, have failed in establishing that they are manufacturers within their own names or in some manner whatsoever and that they have been selling drugs in their respective names or by any other mode whatsoever.

The appellants were partners of a firm carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of drugs. The Income tax Officer held that the appellant was not liable to pay income tax under section 10(2) (xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal reversed the order. In the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal had wrongly held that there was no evidence to show that the appellants were carrying on the business in their own name and that the amount of Rs. 1,50,000/ was not a trading receipt. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the amounts of Rs, 1,51,000 were not trading receipts. [601 D] (ii) The High Court was wrong in holding the appellant liable to tax under s 10(1)(xv). [602 E F] (iii) The finding of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner was erroneous and must be set aside. [703 G] (iv) The fact that the assessee had not been carrying on any business in his own name or in the name of a partner does not make it clear that the said amount was trading receipts, because, the Tribunal has wrongly held the appellant to be a trading asset. [781 D F] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. P. V. Raman & Co., , referred to.

The Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 was passed by the State Government under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Land Acquisition Officer made an award on March 31, 1984 stating that the land in question was acquired for a public purpose and that the acquisition proceedings were initiated after the expiry of the period of six months from the date of the publication of the notification under section 6 of the Act. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said award by filing writ petitions before the High Court which were dismissed by the High court on March 23, 1984. In the appeals to this Court it was contended that the Land Acquisi tion Act, 1985 was not applicable to the case and that since the land had been acquired for public purpose, the acquisition proceeding should have been initiated after expiry of six years from the publication thereof under section 3 of the Acquisition Act. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the proceedings were barred by limitation as it was not filed within six months of the date on which the award was made and that there was no delay in filing the writ petition. [794B] 2. The acquisition proceedings are initiated after a lapse of six year from the commencement of the Amendment Act, 1988. The period of four years is to be computed from the end of the year. The time spent by the petitioners for filing the Writ Petition is not excluded. [774C D] 3. The delay in making the award under section 11 of the 1894 Act is a factor which has to be taken into account while considering the question whether the acquisition was justified or not. [764F G] 4. In view of the fact that the petitioners had filed the writ petitions after the lapse of eight years from that date, it cannot be said that there were any delay in the filing of the Writ Petitions. [754G H; 771A B] 5. The proceedings initiated by the Land acquisition Officer under section 17 of the is not barred by time as the petitioners have filed the Writ petitions after lapse of seven years from this date. [784F] 6. In these circumstances, the High Courts were right in holding that the delay in furnishing the writ Petitions was not bona fide and that it was for the petitioners to approach the High 'Court under section 18 of the .

The appellant, a Bank employee in the Bank, was appointed as an Assistant Manager of the Bank. The Bank made an award on March 31, 1959, awarding inter alia the difference between the pay scale and the dearness allowance payable to the employees. The award provided that the dearness allowances payable to employees shall be fixed at Rs. 1/ per mensem. The appellant contended that the award was not a 'award ' within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, because it was made in accordance with the provisions of the Act and that the appellant had no right to claim any higher pay scale on the basis of the recommendations of the Third Pay Commission. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled to the higher pay scales on the ground that they were not entitled to any higher scale on account of their being appointed as a clerk in the bank. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held (i) that the Tribunal was right in holding that the provisions contained in the award were applicable to the case and (ii) that it was not open to the appellant to claim the higher scale at Rs 1/per mensem. In appeal by special leave, Held:(i) The award was a ' Award within the scope of section 3(b). The award did not contain any provision for fixing the pay scales in accordance therewith. (ii)(a) The Tribunal was wrong in holding (i)(a), (b) and (c) that there was no provision for fixation of the pay structure on the principle of 'equal pay for equal work '. (iii)(a). The Tribunal had not given any reasons for fixing a scale of pay to employees on the footing that they would be entitled to higher pay than what was fixed by the Fourth Pay Commission, and (iv) that in view of the provisions in the Act, the award could not be said to have been made in conformity with the recommendations. The High Court was right In holding that it did not contravene any provision contained in section 2 (b).

The appellants, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913, were granted lease for construction of a hotel. The lease was to expire on June 30, 1981. In the meantime, the Government of West Bengal issued a notification dated May 5, 1981 inviting applications from the owners of the hotel for grant of lease in respect of certain land situated within the city of Calcutta. The appellants submitted their objections to the said notice and stated that they were not willing to accept the offer made by them. The Government of India rejected the objections on the ground that the land was not a commercial building and that the Government had no power to grant the lease in favour of the owners. The State Government, however, refused to accept their objections. The High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to any relief under section 19(1)(f) of the Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the acquisition of land for a commercial purpose was not bona fide and that there was no violation of the principles of natural justice. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the Government was justified in refusing to accept or reject the offer is essentially one of fact and law. [782D] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellants had been granted lease by the Government for a period of five years from the date of the acquisition. They were not ready to accept any offer made on behalf Of the owners in respect thereof. The land was acquired for the purpose of construction of hotel and lodging houses. The acquisition was for a public purpose and it was for the Government to consider whether the land had been acquired for a charitable purpose or for a particular purpose. [771E] 2:2. The decision of the High Court is set aside and the matter remanded to the State Government for fresh consideration on merits. [761F G] 3.3 In the circumstances, the State Govern ment was justified to accept and reject the offers made by the appellants in respect to the land in question. [751G H; 771A B] 4:4. The offer of the appellant was not genuine or bona fide. The appellant had no right to the grant of the lease. [781F] 5:5. The respondent, a Company registered under West Bengal Premises (Regulation and Development) Act, 1956, was entitled to the lease for a residential purpose. The lessee was also entitled to a lease in his favour for a term of five year from the Government. The grant of a lease was not for a limited period.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in the business of buying and selling shares. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee to tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the gift made by the assessee was not genuine and that the assessee had no right to purchase the shares. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that there was no evidence on record to show that the gifts were genuine and were not genuine. In the appeal before this Court it was contended for the Revenue that the High Court was in error in holding that the Gift Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the gift. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The gift made in favour of the asses see was not a genuine gift but was a genuine one and could not be treated as a genuine transaction. [722B] (2) In the instant case, the gift was genuine and was not valid. It was therefore not open to the assessee either to prove that the donor had no title or interest in the property. The High Court rightly held that it was not necessary for the Income tax authorities to assess a gift made under section 11(1)(a) of Indian Income tax Act, 1961. [774C] (3) In view of the fact that the income from the assessee 's own business was not taxable in view of section 10 of the Act, it could not have been said that the transfer was genuine. [764F G] (4) The High Courts were right in holding against the assessee.

The Orissa High Court (Administration of Judicial) Rules, 1962, were framed by the Governor of Orissa under article 309 of the Constitution. The rules were made in exercise of the powers conferred on him by article 309 and the rules were published in the Gazette. Rule 3(1)(a) of the Orissa High Courts (Administration and Judicial) Order, 1962 provided that the High Court shall have jurisdiction to make orders for the transfer of judicial officers and other subordinate courts. The High Court held that the transfer was not a transfer within the meaning of article 309 but was an administrative act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the rules framed by him were ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as they were not in accordance with the provisions of article 235 and were therefore ultra vires. HELD: (i) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to transfer judicial officers or subordinate courts within the purview of article 233. [630 H] (ii) The transfer was a administrative act and it could not be said that the transfers were made by the High Courts in exercise Of their powers under articles 235 and 235. [730 A B] (iii) The rules framed under article 235 are ultra vires and void. They are therefore ultravires. [781 C D] (iv) The power of transfer is a judicial function and it can be said to be administrative act or not. It cannot be said in the absence of any statutory provision that the power of appointment conferred on the High court by article 235 is not an administrative function. [783 A B, F] (v) The rule making authority under article 233 is not a matter of judicial control and it must be held to be a judicial act. It is only when the High courts are entrusted with the functions of the High judiciary that they are entrusted to the High Judges or subordinate Courts. [784 C D; 784 A B]. (vi) The word "judicial" in article 235 means not merely administrative but also administrative, and it includes administrative functions. [830 E] (vii) The expression "judicial act" is used in the context of judicial functions. It has to be understood in its popular sense and in its ordinary sense. [78 C D].

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of a house in Punjab. The respondent purchased the property from one Smt. Surinder Kaur and her husband. The appellant 's father died on 6.1.1960 leaving behind his widow Smt. Mohinder Kaur and his wife Smt. Sohan Kaur. The suit was decreed by the trial court holding that the sale deed dated 4.12.1961, executed by Smt. Surjit Kaur in favour of the respondent was void as it was not a pre emption within the meaning of Article 31(1)(a) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant ' had no right to purchase the property and that the respondent could not be said to have acquired any right under Article 31 (1)(b) of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The sale deed was void on the ground that it was a pre spective sale within the definition of Article 366(22) of Constitu tion. [703B] 2.2 The appellant was not entitled to purchase any property in view of the provisions of Article 39(b) and (c). The respondent 's husband had no locus standi to challenge the sale on the grounds that she was a co sharer of the land. The sale was void because she was not the owner or the vendee. [774C] 3.1 In the instant case, the appellant was the co sharers of the property in question and was entitled to claim the benefit of Article 14 of the Constitu tion on the basis that she had acquired any rights under Article 39 (b) as it stood before the amendment of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1960. [764C D] 3:2 The respondent was not an co sharant of the said property and could not claim the protection of Article 19(1) (a). The appellant having failed to establish that she acquired any title under Article 366 (22) as she had purchased the same from her husband, she cannot be said in possession of the same. [754C E] 3.(i) The High Courts were right in holding that it is not a case where the sale was valid and the appellant could not challenge the validity of the sale by filing a suit for declaration of title on the plea that she purchased the land from her father, as she was the only co sharants. [744C F] (ii) The appellant had no title to the property since she acquired the right under article 31(2)(a). [755G H] 3(i) In the case of a pre pre emptor of a land in question, the sale could not have been declared void on that ground. [784C G] (iii) The respondent had no rights to purchase it from her mother and she was entitled under Article 14.

The petitioner filed a suit for partition of the property in dispute on the ground that he had no interest in the property. The trial court decreed the suit and directed the parties to pay Rs.2,000 as compensation. The petitioner filed an application under Article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioner that the compromise deed had been executed in favour of the respondent and that the decree had been passed without any authority of law and that he was not entitled to any relief as prayed for by him. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The compromise deed has been executed on the basis of a compromise deed which is a part of the family property of the parties. It is true that the parties have agreed that the properties should be sold in their favour and that they will not be entitled to the relief as claimed by them. But, it does not mean that the terms of the compromise are not binding on the parties but only the terms which are binding on all parties. [615E] 2. The High Court has rightly held that the settlement deed had not been executed and that there was no reason for the High Courts to interfere with the order of the trial court. [716F G] 3. In view of the fact that the respondent had agreed to sell the property, it is not possible to hold that the sale deed had already been executed by him in favour thereof. The settlement deed has not been acted upon and the HighCourt has rightly refused to interfere. [781G] 4. The parties have no right to execute the decree in favour or for any other reason whatsoever.

The appellants, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, were employed in the manufacture of sugar. The workmen were paid wages for the period from 1st April, 1969 to 31st March, 1970. The company claimed that the workmen had been allowed to work as a result of which they were not entitled to any benefit under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1957. The Industrial Tribunal held that the employees were entitled to the benefits under the Act and directed the employer to pay the same within six months from the date of the award. On appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that the company was not entitled for any benefit in respect of the period prior to 1st March 1969 and that the benefit under section 10(2) of the Act had been granted to them on the ground that they were entitled only to the benefit of the provisions contained in the Industrial Dispute (Appellate Tribunals) Act. The Tribunal held, inter alia, that the workers were entitled for the benefits of the said Act and not to the extent of the benefit given under section 9(2). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellants are entitled to a benefit of section 10 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act. [795F] 2. The benefit under sections 10(1) and 10(3) is available only when the employer has been allowed the benefit on the basis of the relevant material before it. [774C D] 3. The expression 'any benefit ' in section 10 (2) means a benefit which is granted to an employee on the date on which he was allowed to continue in service. The words 'any benefits ' are not intended to be given to an employer on the same footing as those of a workman who has been dismissed or removed from service. [764F] 4. The word 'any ' occurring in section 2(a) means 'any advantage which is given to a workman on the day on which his discharge is discharged or discharged or dismissed or discharged, or dismissed, or discharged '. [754G H; 771A B] 5. The definition of 'any person ' in the Act has been defined in section 3(a). It means 'all benefits granted to a worker on the grounds that he was entitled to such benefit under any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, express or implied, and includes benefits which are given to him by way of compensation. [ 771C] 6. The term 'any workman ' has been used in the context of the expression 'other person '. It means a person who is dismissed or dismissed from service on the terms of his employment. The meaning of the word 'other persons ' in that section is not to be extended to those who are dismissed or discharge, but to those whose services have been terminated or discharged by reason of the fact that he has been removed from the service. It is only when a workman has been discharged or retrenched that he is entitled to benefits under any law for which he is dismissed, discharged or discharge. [781E F] 7. The object of the definition of `any person" in section 9 (2)(a) is to give benefit to an industrial worker on his attaining the age of superannuation and to provide for the benefit thereunder. It has been held that it is not possible to hold that the expression "other persons" in the definition would mean a person whose services are terminated or dismissed by reason thereof, but only when he has attained the age, the expression `any other person ' would have been given the benefit. [791E G] 8.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the , on the ground that he had been deprived of his personal liberty by an order of detention. The grounds of detention were served on him on the basis of which the order of preventive detention was passed. He challenged the validity of the order on the grounds, inter alia, (i) that the appellant was not a citizen of India and (ii) that he was not entitled to any protection under article 22(5) of his Constitution. Held, that the order was vitiated by mala fides. The order of the Government of Bombay in exercise of its powers under section 8(1)(a) of COFEPOSA was invalid because it was made after the passing of the detention order and the grounds were not supplied to him. The fact that the grounds of the appellant were supplied to the appellant did not make any difference. The appellant had no right to be heard before the order could be passed. The Government of Maharashtra vs The State of Bombay, ; , referred to. Held further, that in a case where the order is made by the Government under section 9(1), it must be shown that the person concerned was not an "public authority" within the meaning of article 22 (5) and that the detention was illegal because the grounds supplied were vague and indefinite. The mere fact that there was no material to show that the detenu was a citizen, does not mean that the Government had made any such order in exercise Of its powers. The only ground which is furnished by the appellant is that he has been deprived or deprived of personal liberty.

The respondent was a member of the Indian Army. He was charged with an offence under section 5(1) read with section 7 of the , and was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct, and that he was not given any opportunity to show cause against his dismissal. The respondent challenged the order of dismissal by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was guilty of professional misconduct and that the order was bad because it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of discharge passed against him is not invalid as it contravenes articles 311(1), 311(3) and 311(4). [657 D] (ii) The respondent was not a member in the Indian Armed Forces. He had been dismissed from the service on account of his dismissal from service. His removal from service was therefore illegal. [658 G H; 630 A B] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the impugned order of compulsory retirement is invalid because it contravenes article 311 (2). [625 D E] (iv) The impugned order is not a punishment under article 311, and the respondent must be given an opportunity to explain his conduct. [625 G H] (v) The power conferred on the Central Government by r. 12 of the Defence of India Rules, 1954, is in the nature of a power conferred upon it by r . 12 of that Act. [600 A B].

The appellant was a Panchayat Samiti. The respondent, who was the Sarpanch of the Gram Panchayat, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the resolution passed by the Panchayat Samiti on March 31, 1964, and prayed for a declaration that the resolution dated March 31. 1964 was invalid as it had not been passed under section 3(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no locus standi to file the appeal within time. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The resolution dated April 31, 1963, was valid and could not be challenged on the ground that it was passed under r. 3(2) of Rule 3(3). [657 D] (ii) The High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal after the expiry of the period prescribed by r. 4(1), but it did not do so. [658 G H; 630 A B] (iii) The appellant was not a Panchayat Panchayat Samiti within the meaning of section 3 (1). [625 D F] (iv) The respondent had no right to file any appeal under r, 3(4). [557 E] (v) The notice dated April 1, 1964 issued by the appellant was invalid because it did so in view of the provisions of section 4(2), and that the notice dated March 1, 1963 was not valid. [625 B C] (vi) The notification dated April 3, 1964 was valid as it was not passed under the Act and therefore the resolution was invalid.

The appellant was convicted by the Labour Court under section 33(1) of the , and sentenced to imprisonment for a term of three years. The High Court confirmed the conviction but acquitted him on appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of section 33 are not intended to be construed in a narrow or pedantic sense. It is only when there is a dispute as to whether the proceedings under section 10(1)(b) of , were pending before the Labour Commissioner and the matter is referred for adjudication by the appropriate Government. [657 H] (ii) The words "in respect of any dispute" in section 33 (1) are wide enough to include only those cases where there is an industrial dispute as regards the existence or otherwise of such a dispute. But if the proceedings are pending before a Labour Commissioner, it would be open to the appropriate government to refer the matter for adjudication under section 11(1). [658 H] The words 'in respect thereof" in sub section (2) are not meant to include those cases which are pending after the date of the reference. But where there are two or more cases pending before an Labour Commissioner the proceedings must be held to have been pending before him and the appropriate authority is bound to refer it for adjudication. [758 H; 758 A] (iii) The word "in regard to" in the section means that the proceedings should be concluded by a conciliation officer, and the conciliation officer may, after giving notice to the parties concerned, submit his report to the Government. If there is no dispute as between the parties, he will be entitled to refer such matter for arbitration under section 12(1), and if the Government so desires, it will be open for the appropriate Govt.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the Bihar Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The order of detention was served on him by the District Magistrate on 21/12/1986. The grounds of detention were served on the detenu on 21st December, 1986 and he was released on bail on 3/2/86. The petitioner challenged the order of his detention before the High Court which dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order passed by the detaining authority was not vitiated because the grounds of preventive detention were vague and indefinite and that the detenu had been detained under section 3(1) of the Act, as he was in jail custody for more than three months and that there was no material before the detaining officer to show that the petitioner was in judicial custody. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not properly appreciated the facts and circumstances of the case and the order is vitiated because it is based on irrelevant considerations. [782B] 2. In the instant case, the grounds served on detenu were vague, indefinite and indefinite. There was no evidence to show how the petitioner had been in judicial detention. The detaining authority has not considered the material before him and has come to the conclusion that there were sufficient materials for making the order. [77C D] 3. In view of the fact that the grounds mentioned in the grounds are vague, the order cannot be sustained. [76D E] 4. The detention order was passed on 21.12.1986 and the detenu was released from jail custody on 3.2.86. There is no material to show what was stated in the order dated 21.11.1986. [75F G] 5. In a case where the detaining authorities have not considered any material before it, the detention order cannot sustain. The fact that there has been sufficient materials before the authority to come to its conclusion on the basis of which the order was made is not a ground for preventive detention. [78E F] 6. There are no cogent reasons for holding that the detaining Authority had not considered all material before he came to the finding that the detention was vitiated because there were material before them to show why the detenu should be released on his executing a bond in favour of his wife and children. The satisfaction of the detaining author is not based on any irrelevant considerations or extraneous consideration.

The appellant firm was carrying on business in gold and silver. The firm had been running a business of selling gold and gold. In the year 1967, the firm had made an application to the Central Government for grant of permission under section 59(1) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 for granting permission to the firm to carry on business as a dealer in gold. The Central Government rejected the application. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the application was not maintainable because the application had been made after the expiry of the period of licence and that the firm was not entitled to grant permission under the Act. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were in error in holding that the provisions of section 59 (1) (a) of Andhra Pradesh Act were ultra vires the Constitution as they contravened articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31 and 31 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding the application for permission to carry out business as an dealer in silver and gold and that it was not a case of violation of article 19(2) (g). [782B C] 2. The question whether the application made by the firm under section 60(1), could be said to have been made within the period prescribed by the statute is no longer res integra. It has been held in this decision that the power conferred on the Central Legislature under Entry 52 of List I, List II, List III, List I and Entry 52, List 1, List 11, List 2, List 3, List 4, List 7, List 8, List 9, List 10, List 14, List 13, List 12, List 17, List 19, List 25, List 18, List 23, List 24, List 26, List 27, List 28, List 29, List 30, List 31, List 32, List 33, List 22, List 21, List 20, List 39, List 36, List 37, List 38, List 40, List 34, List 35, List 44, List 15, List 16, List No. 25, list 27, list 26, list 28, list 30, list 31, list 29, list 33, list 24, list 32, list 22, list 23, list 21, list 25, lists 30, lists 29, and list 31. The power conferred by section 59 of the Act is not confined to the power of the Central legislature under Entry 53, List l, List 6, List 111, List VII, List IV, List 5, List 51, List 52, list 1, list 11, list 7, list 13, list 19, list 14, list 16, list 17, list 18, list 20, list 15, list of 19, lists of 19 and list of 22, lists, list, list and list list of 21, lists and list. [785C D] 3. The provisions of the , are not ultra vires Article 19(3) (f). [882D E] 4. The Act is a self contained code and has no application to any law relating to the subject matter of the legislation. It is not open to the legislature to enact a statute in respect of matters enumerated in List I or List II.

The appellants were the descendants of a Hindu Religious Endowments. The respondents claimed that they had been in possession of certain properties and that they were entitled to possession of those properties as they had not been given any right to the temple. The trial court held that the appellants were entitled only to possession on the ground that they did not possess the right to possession. On appeal, the High Court reversed the findings of the trial court and held that there was no evidence to show that the respondents were in possession or were in actual possession of the properties as their descendants had been given a right to possess the property as they were in continuous possession of them. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the High court was wrong in holding that the suit was barred by article 14 of the Constitution and that the plaintiffs were entitled under article 14. The question whether the respondents could claim possession on a proper construction of the Madras Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, is not one of fact to be decided by the trial Court. The decision of the High Courts in the present case was based on the evidence adduced before it and the High judge was right in holding the suit as barred by Article 14. Held further, that article 14 does not apply to a case where the property is held by a Hindu religious institution or a Hindu undivided family, but it applies only to a particular case where there has been a partition of the joint family properties between the parties and the other where there are no such partition. The suit was therefore barred by articles 14 and 19 of the Limitation Act.

The respondent firm, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the manufacture of electric wires and electric wires. The firm had been running its own business in its name as a licensee under the Jammu & Kashmir Municipal Act, 1911. The partnership firm was dissolved by the District Magistrate, Jammu. The District Magistrate passed an order directing the respondent to remove the electric wires from the premises in question on the ground that the licence granted to it by the Chief Commissioner had been cancelled and the licence had been renewed for a period of one year. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the District Judge, Jammu, contending that the license was not valid because the licence was issued in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the licensee had been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action taken by him under the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the High court in exercise of its powers under section 3(1) of the Jammu and Kashmir Municipal Corporation Act, 1890, was not justified because the license had been issued in violation of the provisions contained in the Act, and that the District Magis trate had no jurisdiction to issue a writ of certiorari quashing the order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed under section 4(1)(a) of Jammu & Ajmer Municipal Corporation Ordinance, 1911 is not valid as it was issued without jurisdiction. [682B C] 2. The power conferred on the District Court by section 3 of the General Clauses Act, 1904 is a discretionary power and the High Courts have no power to issue any writ of mandamus or other appropriate direction in respect of the same matter. [782D E] 3. The powers conferred on a District Magistrate under section 12 of the said Act are not confined to the exercise of his powers under the statute. It is only when the District Magistrates exercise their powers under that Act that they have exercised their discretion and acted in breach of the statutory provisions, that power cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. [781E] 4. The impugned order passed on the basis of the material placed before it by both sides, was a valid one and the same having been passed without jurisdiction, the High 'Court has no power under section 482 of the Code to issue such writ of Mandamus or other suitable direction in regard to the same matters. [783E] 5. The Act does not provide for any special remedy for the aggrieved party to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court under article 226 of the Constitution. It does not contemplate a case where the District and Sessions Judge exercises his powers conferred by section 12, but has exercised his discretion in regard thereto. [784G H; 784A] 6. The provisions contained therein are intended to be construed in a manner which would defeat the very object of the legislation. The object of such a statute is to prevent abuse of the process of the court and to secure justice. It cannot be said that the power conferred by the Act has been exercised arbitrarily and capriciously or capricically with a view to preventing abuse of its process.

The appellants were the owners of certain properties in Bombay. The respondent was a displaced person and the Custodian issued a notice under section 8(1) of the , calling upon them to show cause why the sale should not be cancelled. The appellants challenged the validity of the notice on the ground that it contravened article 14 Of the Constitution as it infringed articles 19, 21 and 31 of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case in which the sale was made. The provisions of section 8 were not intended to be applied to cases where there was a breach of the contract or the rules of natural justice. The words "any person aggrieved by an order under section 9(1), as they stood before the amendment, must be construed strictly and should be interpreted in their ordinary sense. The word "any other person" in section 8 (1) is not intended merely to include a person aggrieved against an order made under section 10(1). The words used in the section are not intended only to include persons aggrieved by any order made by the Custodian under section 11(1)(a), but also to include those who were affected by such order. The expression "any authority" in the context of the definition must be interpreted strictly and construed in their popular sense. It is well settled that a person affected by an action under the Act must be deemed to have been affected by the action taken under section 7(1); it is not necessary that the law should be applied retrospectively, unless there is a clear provision in the statute or the Rules of natural Justice. The object of the amendment was to prevent the abuse of the process of court and to secure the ends of justice. It was not necessary for the Custodian to show that the action under section 6(1A) was intended to affect the rights of the parties, because, the provisions in the Act did not apply retrospectively.

The appellant, a tenant of the land in dispute, was allotted to him by the Revenue Divisional Officer, Jaipur. The Revenue Divisional officer, Jaipur, however, held that the land was not liable to be assessed for the purpose of assessment under section 5(1) (a) of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1950. The appellant filed an appeal before the Board of Revenue which dismissed the same holding that the lands were liable to assessment under the Act and that the Board had no power to assess the land on the basis of the provisions of the Act. The Board also held that since the land had been allotted to the appellant by the revenue Divisional Officer the land could not be assessed to the extent of 50 acres, and that it was not necessary for the Revenue Officer to determine the land under section 4(1)(a) (i) of Rajasthan Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since there was no power under the Rajasthan Land Reforms Act, 1951, the Board could not have assessed the land as a result of which the land would be liable to pay the land revenue. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Revenue officer had no jurisdiction to assess land under the provisions and that he had no authority to assess or reassess the land. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power under section 3 (1) of Act is a discretionary power and not a judicial power. It is an administrative power which has been conferred on the Board by section 4 (1). [501B] 2. The powers of the Revenue Officers are very wide and they cannot be exercised in a manner which is not permissible to do so. They can only be exercised by the subordinate courts or tribunals subordinate to them. It may be possible for the subordinate Courts or tribunals to exercise their jurisdiction under section 17 (1), but that does not mean that the powers of an inferior court are not controlled by any statute or statutory rules. [502C] 3. The Act is intended to provide for the control and regulation of revenue administration and control of revenue and it is a well settled principle of law that the power conferred on them by section 17(1), in respect of matters enumerated in the Act, must be exercised judicially and not arbitrarily or capriciously. [602C D] 4. The provisions of section 5 (1)(b) (ii) of Bihar Tenancy and Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1956 are intended to give effect to the provisions contained in the Rajasthan Revenue Lands Act.

The respondent, a public limited company, was appointed as an Assistant Labour Commissioner in the Central Government under section 3(1) of the , to perform the functions of the Chief Labour Commissioner. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Tribunal and also the order dated March 31, 1982 passed by the Industrial Tribunal, Nagpur. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not an employee of the appellant company and therefore he was not entitled to any relief under section 10(2) of . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the expression "any person" in section 2(1)(a) of , includes a person who is employed by him in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State, and therefore the word "any other person" has been used in the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "other person" means any person who has been employed by a person in connection therewith or incidental to the affairs thereof. [703B] 2. The definition of "any persons" in the definition of 'any person ' is wide enough to include persons who are employed by the Central or State Government, but it does not include persons employed by any other person in relation thereto. It is well settled that the word 'any other word ' includes any person employed by an employer in connectionwith the affairs or incidental thereto. The word "other persons" has a wide connotation and it cannot be said that the definition is wide to include all persons who have been employed in connection directly or indirectly with the work of the Central, State or Union Territory. [771C] 3. The term "anything done by an employee in connection or incidental or ancillary to the work or incidental thereof" has not been defined in the . The expression 'other person ' includes a company engaged in any business or industry which is engaged in the work and the expression 'anything in connection thereto ' means anything done by the employer in relation to the business or undertaking. [761C D] 4. The meaning of the word `any other than those employed in the section is not restricted to persons who were employed by it in connection With the affairs, affairs, business or undertakings. It has been defined as a person engaged in an industry or industry. It includes any work done by him for the purpose of carrying on the work. [751G H] 5. The dictionary meaning of word `other person` is that the words `anything ' are not used in connection only with the business, but also to those who have employed them in connection to the works. It means any thing done by a workman in connection exclusively or for the purposes of carrying out the work, and includes any act done by his employer in pursuance of the work which is done by such person in pursuance thereof. The words `other persons ' are used in relation only to those employed by that person in respect of the works, and not to those engaged in connection solely or for any other purpose. [741G] 6. The concept of `any person` in section 3 (1) (a) is wide and it includes all persons employed in a particular industry or undertaking, including persons employed therein. It does not mean that the term `other than those engaged ' has been given a wider meaning. The definitions of `other ' are wide enough and it is not possible to hold that the expressions `other things ' have been used by the legislature in connection w.e.f. 1st April, 1982. [731G; 74A] 7.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he had been in possession of the premises and that the appellant was not in occupation of the said premises. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the respondent was in occupation since the date of the agreement, and that he was in possession thereof. The High Court held that the suit was not maintainable because the respondent had no right to continue in occupation till the date on which the agreement was executed. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the agreement did not create a new tenancy or a new lease; that the licence was not a license under section 3(1)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947; that since the respondent landlord had no title to the premises, he could not be evicted from the premises. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The agreement did create a tenancy or an additional lease in respect of the demised premises. It was not for the tenant to prove that the premises were let out to him by the licensee. [723B] 2. The respondent landlord was not entitled to continue as a licensee under section 13(1) (a) and (b). The appellant had no locus standi to file the suit. The appellant could not have filed the suit for recovery of possession of premises on the basis that he did not possess any right to remain in occupation until the date when the agreement came into force. [777C] 3. The question whether a licensee was in actual possession or not is essentially one of fact and it cannot be said that he could be evicted only by virtue of section 13 (1) of that Act. [783B C] 4. In the instant case, the respondent did not establish any tenancy or additional lease. The suit was filed on the date the agreement had been executed. The Trial Court held in favour of the respondent and decreed the suit holding that it was a license within the meaning of section 3 (1)(b) of Bombay Rents Hotel and Rates Control (Amendment) Act, 1973. [781B] 5. In view of the finding recorded by the High Court that the licensee had no subsisting right to occupy the premises in question, the appellant could have filed an application under Article 227 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of eviction passed against him. The appeal is dismissed.

The respondent was a Ruler of Rajasthan. He had been granted a permit to the appellant under the Rajasthan Merged States (Taxation Concessions) Order, 1950, by the State of Rajasthan on the ground that he had no authority to grant the permit. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from him as well as for refund of the amounts paid by him in respect of the goods exported by him. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the respondent was entitled to the refund of amounts paid under the contract of sale and that the State had no jurisdiction to grant it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The State could not be said to have acted in a manner which would defeat the provisions of article 31(2) of the Constitution. It is well settled that the law of the land must be construed strictly as having regard to the nature and extent of the liability of the State to pay the amount, the liability being one of the two States. The State cannot be said in a way which would frustrate the provisions Of article 31 (2) and it could not have acted under any other provision of law. [657 H] (ii) The respondent was not entitled to claim refund of money paid by the appellant as well. The liability of a State to make payment of the tax due from the appellant was not one of its liabilities. The question whether the State was entitled or not to claim the refund was not decided in the present case. [757 H; 758 A] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the liability to pay tax under the contracts of sale was a liability of an Indian State and could not, therefore, be said by itself to have been incurred by it.

The appellants, who were dealers in agricultural produce, challenged the validity of the Madras Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1953 (Act No. IV of 1952) on the ground that they contravened article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and that the provisions of section 5 of the Act infringed articles 14 and 19(2) of Part III of the constitution. The High Court held that the impugned Act was ultra vires the State Legislature and that it violated article 19 (1)(f). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The impugned Act is a colourable legislation and is not within the competence of the State legislature under Entry 52 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. It is therefore not open to the appellants to challenge the validity or legality of the impugned provisions on the grounds that they infringed articles 19(3)(g). [775 G] (ii) The Act is not a colourable one and is therefore ultra vires article 19. [776 H; 776 A B] (iii) The object of the legislation is to provide for the regulation of trade, commerce and intercourse with the community. It cannot be said that the Act was intended to give effect to the provisions contained in section 5(1). [774 D E] (iv) The objects of the statute are not to provide a reasonable basis for the classification of the goods or services rendered by the manufacturers. The object is to prevent the abuse of the power and to secure the equitable distribution of trade and commerce. It may be that the Legislature has made it obligatory on the State Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the law relating to trade, business, commerce, intercourse and intercourse.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the evidence of P.Ws. 2, 3 and 4 could not be relied upon as they were interested witnesses; (ii) the fact that the evidence was not corroborated by any other evidence would not make them liable for conviction under section 34; (iii) the High Court erred in holding that the testimony of P,W. 5 could not have been acted upon because he had no motive to commit the crime; and (iv) the conviction was based on circumstantial evidence. HELD : The High Courts were right in holding the appellants guilty of murder. [738 B] In the present case the evidence did not show that the appellants were interested persons. It was not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the accused had any motive to kill the deceased. The fact that P,Ws. 3 and 5 were interested witness could not make it liable for the conviction under sections 302 readwith section 34. [771 C] In view of the evidence on record it is clear that the High Courts have taken a different view in regard to the evidence adduced by the prosecution. It is well settled that the Court has to take into consideration the circumstances of each case and not the circumstances which are peculiar to the accused. The circumstances of the case must be such as to exclude every hypothesis but they must be so consistent with the innocence of the accused and must be consistent only with his innocence.

The petitioner was appointed as a temporary Assistant Engineer in the Department of Public Works Engineering. He was promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer on 1.1.1976. His services were terminated by an order dated 31.3.1977. The petitioner challenged the said order before the High Court which held that the order of termination was not in accordance with law and therefore, it was not open to him to challenge the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the impugned order was passed without giving any opportunity to the petitioner to show cause against the proposed action of the Government. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The order of compulsory retirement is a condition precedent for the exercise of power under Article 311(2) of the Constitution and cannot be said to have been passed without affording him an opportunity to showcause against the impugned orders. [703E] 2.1 In the instant case, the petitioner was not appointed as Superintending Engineer in his Department of Personnel & Training but he had been promoted to that post on 1st January 1976. He had been given a salary of Rs.5,000/ and therefore he could not be said that he had become a permanent Government servant. [774G] 2:2 The order dated 1.3 .1977 was passed by the Chief Engineer in consultation with the Public Works Department and the petitioner having been promoted as Superintending Engineers on 1 st January 1976, he cannot claim any right to continue in service till his retirement. [764C D] 2(a) The order is not a condition of service but it is an order of punishment which can be passed without assigning any reason. It is only when the Government servant has been given an opportunity of showing cause against his proposed action. In the present case, there was no provision in the Rules for compulsory retirement on 1/1st January 1977. The impugned order dated 3.3,.1977 was not a rule and it could not have been issued without giving him any opportunity of being heard. [754G H] 2.(b) The petitioner has been appointed as Executive Engineer in a Department of the Public Health Engineering. His service is governed by the Rules which are applicable to the case of the peti tioner. He has been promoted on 1 1st February 1976 and he has been confirmed in that post. His appointment was not challenged by any person other than the petitioner. The question whether the impugned action was justified or not does not arise for consideration in this Court. [744G; 771A] 2 (a) In the case where a Government servant is appointed on 1nd January 1976 and his services are governed by Rule 3(b), it is open to the Government to pass an order under clause (c) of sub rule (2) after giving him an option to continue as Superintending Engi neer. [784G, 771C D; 772A] (b) In case the petitioner has not been given any opportunity, he may be heard in person or through a representative of the Union Public Works department. [793E F] 2 2(c) The impugned action is not in consonance with law. It was therefore not open for him to contend that the said decision is not applicable to him because he had already been appointed on 3rd January 1976 as Superintending engineer.

The appellant, a deceased employee of the respondent Corporation, was insured with the Life Insurance Corporation of India. The deceased died on September 30, 1964 leaving behind two sons and daughters. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to them from the respondents. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the deceased had not been paid the premium and that the claim was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that there was no negligence on the part of the deceased, and that there were no negligence or failure on the record to prove that the death of the appellant was due to the negligence of the respondents, and as such the claim could not be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in holding the appellant guilty of negligence on his part. [730F] 2. The policy of insurance is a policy of life insurance and it is for the Corporation to satisfy itself that the policy of the Corporation is genuine. It is not necessary that the premium should be paid by the deceased. The premium must be paid in accordance with the policy. If the policy is genuine, the policy will have to be taken into consideration. [771F] 3. The contract of insurance was for a period of two years and it was for the corporation to satisfy the Court that the life insurance was genuine. The Corporation has not been able to prove the fact that the contract of Insurance was genuine or that there is no negligence in the conduct of the employee. [761F G] 4. The claim of the appellants was rightly rejected by the trial court and the High court was right in holding it to be barred by time.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of certain sums due to him from the appellants. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was barred by limitation and that the appellant had no locus standi to file the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that the trial court was not competent to entertain the suit because it was not a court within the meaning of article 136 of the Constitution. On appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that section 141(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure is applicable only where there are two or more parties to the dispute and the matter is one which has been referred to a larger Bench. [657 H] (2) In view of the decision of this Court in M/s. B. D. Dhande & Co., Ltd. vs The State of Bombay, ; , it was open to the High Courts to entertain a suit on the ground that the matter was one which had been referred by a larger bench. [757 H; 758 A] (3) In the present case, the trial Court was not right in rejecting the contention of the appellant that the respondent 's suit was not barred by time and that it was barred under article 136. [781 B C] (4) The trial Court had no jurisdiction to entertain such a suit because the High court had no power to entertain it on the basis of the provisions of section 141.

The respondents are manufacturers of cotton fabrics. They manufacture the same goods as they were manufactured by them in the factory of the Respondents. The Respondents claimed that the value of the cotton fabrics was not includible in the assessable value of such goods. The Respondent filed a Writ Petition before the High Court challenging the validity of Rule 5 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 and also the order of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the respondents were manufacturers of the said goods as the same were manufactured out of the raw material used in the manufacture of the same. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the Respondents were not manufacturers of such cotton fabrics and that they were not entitled to the benefit of Rule 4 of the Rules. Dismissing the Petition, HELD: 1. The respondents are engaged in the manufacturing process of the Respondent and the value thereof is includible in assessable value. [415F] 2. The petitioners are manufacturers in the process of manufacture of cotton fabric. They are also engaged in any manufacturing process. They do not manufacture the said cotton fabrics as they are manufactured out or sold by them. They have to be treated as a manufacturer of such fabrics. [416G H] 3. The value of cotton yarn is includible for the purpose of Rule 6 of the rules. The cost of the goods is to be borne in mind by the manufacturer and the manufacturer. [414C D] 4. The duty of excise is on the manufacture or production of the finished goods. It is not necessary that the goods should be manufactured out from the factory gate. [413D E] 5. Rule 6 does not contemplate any activity which is carried on in the business of the manufacturer, but only a manufacturing process which is done by the manufacturers. The fact that the manufacturer has to maintain accounts and account books for the relevant period would not make it possible to hold that the cost of such manufacture should be included in the value. The manufacturer may also be required to maintain account books as he may have to maintain separate accounts and accounts for the period from 1st April, 1988 to 31st March, 1988.

The appellant was appointed as a Panchayat Samiti in the State of Haryana. He was confirmed in the post of Panchayat Samiti on January 1, 1973. On July 2, 1973 he was appointed to the post by the State Government under section 3(1) of the Punjab Panchayat Raj Act, 1953. The appellant was promoted as Panchayat Samiti from April 1, 1974. In the year 1973 he had been appointed to a post in the Panchayat Samiti. He continued to be in service till July 2. 1973 when he was absorbed in the Gram Panchayat. On June 29, 1973, he was confirmed on the post. His services were terminated by the Panchayat Raj Department. The Panchayat Raj Officer filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had been absorbed in a Panchayat Panchayat Samiti under section 2(1)(a) of Punjab Panchayat Act, 1954. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of the Haryana Panchayat Raj (Amendment) Act, 1973 were not applicable to him because he was not appointed to any post in his Panchayat Samiti and was not a member of the Panchayat Panchayat. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'post" used in section 2 (1)(b) of that Act means a post which is held by an officer or authority under the Panchayat Act. [630B] 2. The expression 'post ' includes a post held by a person who has been appointed as Panchayat Samitis and is not a servant of the Government. It is only when a person is appointed to another post in that Panchayat Samiti, he cannot be said to have been appointed on the same post. [731C D] 3. The definition of 'post under section 1(1), of the 1961 Act is wide enough to include a post not held by him but merely because he has been recruited as Panchayat Pramukh and is appointed in that post. It does not mean that a person cannot be appointed on a different post. The term 'post means a Post held by another person who is appointed as an officer of the same department or authority. [781E] 4. The words "post" in section 1 (1) are wide enough and it includes a Post which is not held for the purpose of the present case.

The appellants were the Mahant of a temple. The property was dedicated to the deity by the deity for the purpose of worship and for the benefit of the deity. The deity was in possession of the properties. The trustees filed a suit against the appellants for possession of their properties. During the pendency of the suit, the deity died leaving behind two sons and three daughters. The appellants were brought on record as defendants. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the property was not dedicated to any religious purpose. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the properties were dedicated for worship and that the deity was entitled to possession of its properties under section 12(1) (a) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that the temple was not a religious purpose but was a religious institution. [612 D] In the instant case, the property belonged to the temple and it was dedicated for the worship and the deity had no right to possession thereof.
