It was therefore not necessary to prove that the income of the temple is not the property of the idol. The High court was in wrong in holding the properties as a religious or charitable institution. The properties were not dedicated for religious purposes. [712 D E] In view of the fact that the appellants had been brought on the record as defendant, it could not be said that they were not entitled to any possession of it.

The appellants were allotted land in the Punjab Government under section 4 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954. The allotment was made on the basis of a notification issued by the Custodian under section 6(1) of the Act. The appellants applied for allotment of their lands to the Custodian but the Custodian rejected the application. The Custodian rejected it. On appeal the Custodian held that the appellants were entitled to allotment of land in accordance with the provisions of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The order was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Custodian had no power to cancel the allotment made under section 5(1). HELD : (i) The Custodian could not cancel the allotments made under the provisions Of the Act if the Custodian has reason to believe that the land is needed for a public purpose. The object of the notification was to prevent the evacuee from taking any action against the appellants and to prevent him from taking action against them. The power conferred on the Custodian by section 6 (1) was not confined to the power of cancellation of allotment made in favour of the Custodian. [723 H] (ii) The order of the High court is set aside and the application for allotment made by the appellants under section 7(1)(a) must be dismissed. [774 D E] (iii) The appellants were not entitled to any allotment under section 3(1), because, the Custodian was in error in holding that the allotment was illegal.

The appellants were appointed as teachers in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Public Service Commission, after considering the objections of the candidates and the candidates, recommended the names of the successful candidates for appointment to the post of Principal. The State Government rejected the recommendation of the Public Service Commis sioner. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Public Services Commission had no power to make appointments in accordance with the rules and the rules. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had no jurisdiction to make appointment in accordance therewith and that the selection made by the Public service Commission was vitiated by mala fides and that there was no violation of any principle of natural justice. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The appointments were made in accordancewith the rules of recruitment and the Rules. The selection had been made in conformity with the Rules and the Public services Commission had not given any opportunity to the candidates to make their representations. [730F] 2. The appointment was made in violation of the rules but there was nothing on record to show that the appointments were mala fide or that the State Government had no authority to make such appointments. [781G] 3. The procedure for selection is not followed by a candidate who has been selected and appointed as Principal. It is only when the Public Commission has given notice of the fact that the candidates have been selected, the Public Sector Undertakings are bound to give them an opportunity to make representations. The public sector undertakings are bound by the rules made in this behalf. [783G] 4. The Commission had also not given a hearing to the appellants and the High Courts had not taken into consideration any of the relevant factors which would justify the selection. [784F] 5. The appellants have been denied the opportunity to be heard. They are entitled to be considered for appointment as Principal in accordance to the rules, if they so desire. [777G] 6. The writ petitions are dismissed. No costs.

The appellant, who was the Mahant of a Hindu Religious Trust, filed a suit for partition and recovery of possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no right to sue in his name. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the rule of primogeniture is applicable only where the person who has been appointed as a Mahant of an institution, is not entitled to sue for the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rule of lineal primogen generis is applicable where the persons who have been appointed in the institution are not entitled under the rules of prim primogenciation. [630B] 2. In the instant case, the appellant was a Mahant and he had no locus standi to sue. He was only a Mahant. His right to institute the suit was not affected by the rule. The appellant could not be said to have been a Mahant in his capacity as a trustee of the institution. [730C] 3. In view of the fact that the rules were applicable, the High Court rightly held that the plaintiff had no title to the properties and he was entitled to institute it. [781E F] 4. The rules of linealogeniture are applicable only when the person appointed as an Mahant is not a member of the Hindu Religious Trusts. [783B C] 5. In order to attract the rule, the rule must be strictly construed. It is well settled that in a case where a person has been nominated as a member, he cannot be said as a successor in interest of the deceased or his successor in office. The right to prosecute is not affected because the rule is applicable when the legal representative of the party who has died and the legal representatives are not parties thereto. [784E F; 784A] 6. In a suit instituted by a person claiming to be an heir, he must be deemed to have become a member or his heirs. The plaintiff cannot claim any right to continue in possession of property until he is appointed as such. [777B C].

The appellant, a member of the Andhra Pradesh State Legislative Assembly, was compulsorily retired from service on March 31, 1982. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification dated December 30, 1983 under section 3(1) of the , which provided that the age of retirement for the purpose of pension shall be fixed by the Governor in consultation with the Commission. In exercise of the powers conferred by sub rule (2) of Rule 4 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, the Governor issued a Notification dated December 31, 1983, under which the age limit of retirement was to be fixed for the purposes of pension. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it had been made in violation of Article 16 of the Constitu tion and that the Government had no power to make any order imposing a major penalty on the members of the service, and that it was not open to the Governor to make an order imposing major penalty. The High Court held that the impugned notification violated article 311(2) and that there was no violation of article 14. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the State Government had acted in violation Of Article 16 inasmuch as the impugned Notification did not contain any provision for the compulsory retirement of a member on the basis of his age. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notification was issued under section 4(1)(a) of that Act and the impugned order was passed without giving any opportunity to the members to show cause why it should not be made in accordance with the provisions of Article 311(3). [782C] 2. The State Government has acted in contravention of the provisions contained in article 16 inasmuch it is not open for the Governor under sub rule(2), to make a law imposing major penalties on members of service, or to impose minor penalty on members who had attained the age prescribed by the said proviso. [785C] 3. The power conferred by Article 309 is not confined to compulsory retirement but only to compulsory retire a member after attaining the age specified in the proviso. It is not permissible for the State to make such an order under sub section (2), if it is made in contravention with the express provision of Article 309, to impose major penalty and to impose a minor penalty. [771C] 4. The validity of this notification was challenged on the grounds that the power conferred upon the Governor by sub clause (2)(a), being arbitrary and violative of article 16, was not available to the State in view of the fact that the said power had been exercised arbitrarily and without any authority of law. [761C D] 5. The contention that the Governor had acted under sub cl (2A) of Article 166 is not tenable because it was made in breach with the statutory provisions of the Act, and since the impugned notifications were issued in violation thereof, the impugned orders are liable to be quashed. [753F G] 6. The question whether the impugned Notifications were invalid or not was a matter which could be decided by the Government under sub clause(2A). [764C D; 771E F] 7. It was open to a State Government to make appropriate orders for compulsory retirement in accordance therewith, and if it so desired, it may consider the question of compulsory retirement. The decision of the Government on the question whether it was necessary to make the impugned impugned order invalid or inoperative is not a matter within the competence of the Governor. [781E G] 8. It could be said that the President had acted arbitrarily and in violation with the principles laid down by this Court, and therefore, the decision of this Court in A.V.S.

The appellants, who were dealers in tobacco, purchased the goods from their customers and sold them to the purchasers. The sales tax authorities held that the sale of the goods was not taxable under section 2(f) of the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1948. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions filed by the assessees. In appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sales tax Authorities had no jurisdiction to levy sales tax on the sale or purchase of the said goods and that the expression "sale" in section 2 (f) means sale of goods, and that section 3(1)(a) of Act 1 of 1948 is not attracted. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: The High Courts were right in holding that the words "sale of goods" in Section 2(g) are not confined to sale of any goods but only to sale or sale of such goods. [742C] In the instant case, the sales Tax Authorities had jurisdiction to assess the sales of the two categories of goods under section 3 (1)(b) of Punjab Sales tax Act, 1947. The appellants were not dealers in the said two categories. They were not entitled to levy tax on sale or purchases of the same goods. The Sales Tax authorities have no jurisdiction in holding the sales. [781E] In view of the fact that the High Court had held that sales tax was payable by the appellants under section 4(1) (a) and (b).

The appellants were dealers in oil seeds and oil. The goods were sold by the respondent to the appellant on the basis of a contract entered into between them for sale of oil seeds. The sales were made on the ground that they had been selling oil seeds but were not liable to pay sales tax under section 3(1) (a) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947. The appellants contended that the sales were not taxable as they were not entitled to exemption under section 4(1)(a). Held, that the sale was not a sale within the meaning of article 286(2) of Part B of the Constitution and the goods were not exempt from tax under the Bombay General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1956. The words "any person who has been assessed to sales tax" in section 3 (1)(b) are wide enough to include a person who is assessed to tax under that Act. The word "any other person" in article 286 (2) means any person who was assessed to the sales tax and includes a person whose goods were subjected to tax by reason of his being assessed to such sales. The expression "any goods" in the definition of "any property" is not defined in the Act as meaning any property which has been declared to be an evacuee or a part thereof. It is well settled that the word "person" in Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution means any property belonging to the person who had been assessed under the Act and includes any person whose property was declared to have been declared as an evacuee. The definition of the term "person", in section 2(1), is wide enough, to include any person whom he has been subjected to sales or purchase by reason thereof. The meaning of the word 'person" is that the expression "person ' includes any other person who may be assessed under that law. It would not be correct to say that the words "person in section 4 (1) are wider than those used in the section.

The appellant, a Hindu, was married to the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for divorce on the ground that she had been living separately and that she was not entitled to maintenance under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had failed to prove her case beyond reasonable doubt. On appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The respondent has not proved her case in any manner whatsoever. She is entitled to maintain herself and she is entitled only to maintenance at the rate of Rs. 100 per month. [775G] 2.2 In the instant case, the appellant was living separately for a period of two years. She had been residing separately for more than three years. The wife has not filed any application for maintenance under the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act. The husband has not shown that she has been living with her. [771C] 3.3 In the absence of any evidence to show that the respondent was living in a separate house, it is difficult to accept the contention that the wife had been staying separately for two years and that the husband had not filed an application for divorce under section 127 of the Act. [762F G] 4.4 The appellant has failed to establish her case. The appellant cannot be allowed to maintain her claim under section 126 of the Indian Penal Code. [753C D] 5.5 In the present case, there is no evidence to prove that the marriage was performed by a Hindu or any other person. The fact that the parties have not filed their respective statements in support of their claims does not make it clear that the relationship between the husband and wife has been established. [741G] 6.6 In the circumstances, the order of the trial court is set aside and the appellant is directed to pay maintenance at Rs. 50 per month to the appellant. The appeal is allowed.

The appellant, a private limited company, was granted a licence for selling liquor to the respondent. The appellant applied for cancellation of the said licence and the Collector rejected his application on the ground that he had no locus standi to file the writ petition. The State Government by its order dated 27th July, 1988 directed the Collector to consider the appellant 's representation in accordance with law. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of cancellation. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under the order dated 26th July 1988. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order dated 25th July 1989 is set aside and the appellant is directed to consider his representation in terms of the order passed by the Collector. [775G] 2.2 In the instant case, the appellant had no right to challenge the order on the grounds that he was not a party to the writ proceeding. The order of the State Government dated 27 th July 1988 is set at naught and the State has no power to cancel the said order. [771C D] 3. The question whether the appellant could be granted any relief in terms thereof is essentially one of fact. It is well settled that a person who seeks to challenge an order passed under the authority of law must satisfy the court that he is not a necessary party. In the present case, there was no violation of any fundamental right or the rules. [761C] 4. The Government has no jurisdiction to cancel or modify the order. It has power to do so in the interest of justice and equity.

The respondents, who were the owners of a building in which they had been let out to the appellant, filed a suit for eviction on the ground that they had acquired title by virtue of an agreement dated 30.9.1958, and that the respondents had no right to recover possession of the property from them. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable as it was barred by limitation under section 14(1)(c) of the . In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that there was no bar for the jurisdiction of the Rent Controller to entertain a suit. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the suit is barred by time under section 13(1) (c) is not one of fact and law. [775G] 2. Section 14(2)(c), however, does not confer any right on the landlord to recover the possession of a property in which he has been let. It does not create any bar for a suit to recover it from the tenant. The jurisdiction of a Rent Controller is limited to the question whether there was an agreement between the parties and the question of limitation under the Act is one of law. In the instant case, the respondents were not entitled to recover any possession from them on the basis of the agreement dated 29.9,.1958. [771C] 3. The High Court was right in holding the suit as barred by section 14 (1)(b) of tho Act. [762F G] 4. Section 13(3) (a) of that Act is a self contained code and does not provide for any bar to the jurisdiction on the question. It is only when the landlord has obtained possession of property in respect of which he is entitled to claim possession, the tenant cannot ask for a decree for eviction. [751G] 5. The provisions of section 14 are intended to be construed strictly and in consonance with the well settled principles of law that the jurisdiction conferred by the Act on the Rent Control Tribunal under the . can be exercised only when there is an agreement or between the landlord and the tenant, and not where there is a relationship of landlord and tenant. [741G H] 6. The right to claim a decree in respect thereof is a matter which has to be determined by the Rent control Tribunal. It cannot be said that the Act does not contemplate any bar on the jurisdiction under section 19(2) (b). [753C D] 7. Section 15(3)(c ) of the Act provides for an appeal against the order of eviction passed by the Controller in respect whereof a decree has been passed by a Court of competent jurisdiction. The words "any question arising in any proceeding" are not intended to include a question which is referred to in section 14. [731G; 742A] 8. Section 16(3), however does not make any distinction between the right and title of the landlord or tenant, but only provides for a remedy by way of an appeal under section 15(4). The words 'any question arises as to whether there is any relationship of master and servant between the tenant and the landlord. [ 741G G] 9. Section 17(3A) (d) of Act does make it clear that the right to sue in respect Of a building or a part thereof has been conferred by section 15 (2). The right of the tenant to claim the decree is not a matter of right and the right of appeal is not an absolute right.

The appellant was appointed as a Forest Officer in the State of Mysore. He was promoted to the post of Forest Officer on March 31, 1967. The respondent challenged the validity of the seniority list and contended that the seniority lists were not vitiated by any violation of principles of natural justice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent had no locus standi to challenge the seniority in question. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the respondent was a Forest officer, he could not be promoted to that post on the ground that he had been given an opportunity to represent his case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The impugned seniority list is vitiated by violation of principle of natural Justice. [630F] 2. The State Government has no power to issue any direction for making a representation against the proposed action. It is not open to the State Government to issue such directions as it may deem fit and proper. [730G H; 730A B] 3. The Central Government has the power to make rules in respect of matters enumerated in List I. The power to frame rules is subject to the control of the Central Government. It does not contemplate any procedure for making an order. The procedure prescribed by law is a statutory one and it cannot be said that the Central Govern ment had no power under the Act to issue directions for making such orders. [830F G] 4. The question whether the respondent has been given opportunity of hearing or not is a matter which must be determined on the basis of the material before him.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of goods in the country, had imported certain goods from different countries and exported them to various countries. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said order by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High court on the ground that the import licence granted to them was not valid because the import policy was not applicable to the case of the petitioners. In appeal, this Court held that the export licence granted under the Import Policy was valid and could not be said to have been valid since the import had been made in violation of the Import Trade Control Policy. The Division Bench also held that there was no provision for grant of a licence to the petitioners for the import of goods from other countries. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts were wrong in holding that the petitioners were entitled to the benefit of the Export Policy and that the said policy was applicable only to the cases where the import was made in contravention of the Imports Control Order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding the impugned order as invalid because it had not been passed in violation or in violation thereof. [703B] 2.1 In view of the fact that the Import policy was valid for the reason that the Export Licence granted to the petitioner was not a valid licence, the HighCourt was wrong in directing the respondents to grant the benefit under the Export policy. [774C D] 2:2 The petitioners were not entitled to any benefit under Export Policy. They had also been granted the benefit by virtue of the order dated 20th July, 1986 passed by this Court in Writ Petition No. 994/86. The said order was made applicable only in respect of cases where import was effected in violation and in violation whereof the petitioners had been granted a licence for the export of goods. [764C] 2 :3 In view thereof, the petitioners are entitled to benefit under para 5 of the Policy. [754F G] 3:4 The petitioners have not challenged the order of the Single Judge dated 20.7.1986 in Writ Appeal No. 894/87 and the said judgment has been affirmed by this court in SLP No. 1094/88.

The appellant is a manufacturer of cotton fabrics. The goods were manufactured by the appellant for sale and purchase of cotton yarn. The appellant claimed that the value of the cotton fabrics was not includible in the assessable value of such goods as the value thereof had been determined under section 4(1)(a) of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the price of the goods was not included in the taxable value of a particular commodity and that the appellant had no right to take the value at which it was sold. The Appellate Tribunal held that the cost of packing of cotton fabric was includible in assessable value under section 3(1) (a). On appeal, the High Court held that there was no evidence on record to show that the goods were not included within the taxable turnover of the appellant and that they were liable to pay duty on the value. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression "value" in section 4 (1) of Central Excise Rules, 1944 means the price which is determined under the provisions of the Act. The expression 'value" has been used in the context of the definition in section 2(g) of that Act. It is well settled that the word "value ' includes the value which is fixed by the statute and not the value as the basis for determining the assessable price. [703F] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant was a manufacturer and the goods are not included under the definition of the expression in section 3 (1)(b) of Act. Therefore, the value determined under Section 4(3) of Excise Act is includible in its assessable value. [774G H; 703A] 1:3 The Tribunal has rightly held that it was a case where the goods have been sold by the assessee to the buyer and not as the price at which the goods had been sold, but the price fixed under Section 3(2) of . The Tribunal is right in holding that the sale price of cotton cloth was includible for the purpose of determining the value under Section 5(1). [775G H] 1 :4 In the case of a manufacturer who sells cotton fabrics to another buyer and sells cotton fabric to another seller, the price determined under Rule 4(2)(a), is not includible for any purpose. The Tribunal was right in taking the view that the market value of cotton goods has been fixed by reference to the value fixed under section 5(3). [704B C] 1.(a) In the present case, there was a difference between the price and the cost which was determined under sub section (1), and the price actually paid. The price fixed for the goods is not the price charged for the sale of cotton. The value of these goods has to be determined in accordance with the provisions contained in Section 4 (3) and the value so determined is the price fetched by the buyer. [764C] 1(b) In view of the fact that the prices fixed under sub clause (a) are not includible, the assessable turnover of cotton cotton fabrics would not be includible for determining whether the cost was includible or not.

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal breach of trust and for having committed a breach of contract. The prosecution case was that he had been given a bribe by the appellant to the Inspector of Police, who had visited the school on the night of the occurrence. The Inspector of police, who conducted the raid, found the appellant guilty of the offence under section 409 IPC. He was also charged with having committed the offence punishable under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs. 500/ . On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt and that the evidence of the witnesses was not corroborated by any other evidence. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had committed the breach of the trust and that he was guilty of criminal misconduct. [775F] 2. The appellant had been convicted under section 420 IPC and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for a period of one year. He had been acquitted by the trial court. The conviction and sentences were upheld by the High court. [771C D] 3. The charge against the appellant was that the money was given to him by the Inspector in connection with the alleged offence. The evidence of PW 1, who was a teacher in the school was not supported by any evidence. The recovery of the money from the appellant is proved beyond reasonable doubts and it cannot be said that he has committed the crime. [761C] 4. The presumption under section 6(2) of Prevention of Anti Corruption Act is not weakened by the presumption. It is a rebuttable presumption. The burden of proving the charge is on the prosecution to prove that the accused had committed an offence. In the instant case, the appellant has failed to establish that he committed the criminal breach. [751G] 5. The onus of proving that the amount was given by the Manager in connection therewith was not discharged by the prosecution. The fact that PW 1 had been paid a bribe is not established. The mere fact that the Manager had been paying the money does not make it clear that he did not pay the money to the appellant. [741G H] 6. In view of the presumption under Section 6(3) of Act, the burden of proof lies on the accused to prove his case beyond reasonable reasonable doubt. The court has to examine the evidence in order to find out whether the amount given by PW 1 was a bribe or not is not sufficient to sustain the conviction. [781C E] 7. In order to establish the charge under section 4(2)(d), it must be shown that the person who had paid the money had been made a bribe, and that this presumption has been rebutted by the accused. The question of proof is whether the burden rests on the appellant or not. [791G; 79A] 8. In a case where the evidence is not corroborated in material particulars, it must also be shown to have been established beyond reasonable suspicion that the sum was given as bribe. [801F G] 9. The Court has to see whether the accused has committed an act of criminal nature or has committed any offence. It may be proved beyond doubt that the gratification was given for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the Act.

The petitioner company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. The respondent company was served with a notice of demand for payment of compensation to the petitioner company on the ground that the company had committed breach of trust and that the Company had failed to comply with the provisions of section 13(2) of the Act. The petitioner company filed an application before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of termination of service of the respondent company. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner was not a 'public servant ' within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of that Act and that it was not entitled to any protection under section 13 (2). Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'public servants ' in section 2 (1)(e) of this Act means 'any person who is in possession or control of property or has been in occupation or has ceased to be a public servant within the definition of section 3(1) (d) and that therefore the word 'public ' in sub section (2) must mean 'a person who has ceased or has become a public servants within the scope of section 12. [794B] 2. The words 'public officer ' in clause (e) are wide enough to include a person who was in possession of property and has ceased, if he is in occupation of any property or had ceased to occupy it for a period longer than three months. The word 'Public servant ' in the context of section 10(2)(d), therefore, means 'a public servant '. [774C] 3. The definition of 'public office ' in Section 2 (i) of section 1 (1) of Act is wide enough and includes a person whose possession or right to occupy the property has been taken over by the company for a long time. It is not possible to hold that the expression 'Public officer ' is wide, but it is wide to include any person who had ceased or had become a member of the public service within the ambit of section 11(2). [775G H] 4. The question whether a public officer ' has been defined in the Act as meaning a person belonging to a scheduled caste or scheduled tribe or scheduled tribes or scheduled castes or scheduled Tribes or scheduled Tribe or scheduled caste, is not a matter for consideration before this Court.

The appellant was the founder of a temple. He had been carrying on business as a trustee for the temple. The appellant was a public trust and was declared elected to the office of the Commissioner. The respondent filed an application under section 47(1) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 for setting aside the order of the District Judge. The High Court held that the appellant had been rightly declared elected as a public trustee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the respondent was not a public servant within the meaning of section 2(e) of Act, and that the order passed by the District judge was without jurisdiction. HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding the order as invalid because it had been made under section 48(1)(a) of that Act. [808 D] (ii) The order of a District Judge is not based on any evidence and the High court erred in taking into consideration the evidence adduced by the parties. [889 E F] (iii) The appellant 's case was that he had been declared elected under section 49(1). He had not been declared as a private trustee within the definition of section 3(e), because, he had not made any such declaration in his favour. The order passed on the basis of the evidence led by the respondent could not be sustained. [879 E] (iv) The finding of the High Courts that the temple was a private trust is not correct.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. The order was served on him by the Collector of Bombay on the ground that he had committed an offence under section 5(2)(a) of that Act and that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to him as he had been convicted for an offence punishable under section 7 of the Indian Penal Code. The petitioner challenged the validity of the order on the grounds, inter alia, (i) that the order was bad because it contravened article 14 of the Constitution; (ii) that in view of the provisions contained in article 22(5) of Part III of the Constitu tion, the order of detention was invalid and inoperative. Held, that the impugned Act was not violative of article 14 inasmuch as it violated articles 14 and 19 of the constitution and was therefore void under article 31A of the Consti tution; (iii) that section 5 of the , did not contravene article 14 because it infringed article 14 and was not unconstitutional. The provisions of Part IV of the said Act were ultra vires article 14, inasmuch as they contravened articles 14, 19 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution. The impugned Act had no application to the case of the petitioner. The question whether the impugned order was invalid or inoperative because it violated article 14 was not decided by this Court in K. M. D. Chamarbaugwala vs State of Bombay, ; , followed. (iv) that even if the impugned provision contravened articles 19 and 31(1), it could be said that the Act violated article 19(2) of its Constitution.

The respondents, who were workmen of the appellant company, filed a petition under section 33C(2) of the , for a direction to the appellants to pay wages for the period during which they worked. The Tribunal held that the respondents had not been able to work out the minimum wages prescribed by the Rules and that the minimum wage prescribed by r. 4 was not exceeded. On appeal, the Tribunal held in favour of the respondents. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal has no power to fix minimum wages for a period of three months under r. 5(1)(b) of Part I of the Rules. [408 C] (ii) The minimum wage is not exceeded by the employer in fixing minimum wages. The minimum wages fixed by r, 4 is not excessive and that it is not necessary to fix any minimum wage for a particular period. The fact that the workmen are unable to work on the minimum rates does not make them liable to pay the minimum minimum wages under r, 5(2). [409 D] (iii) The respondents were not able to carry out the maximum wage prescribed in r. 6(1) of Schedule I to the Rules for fixing minimum wage. They are entitled to a minimum wage under r., 5(3). [508 F G] (iv) The provisions of r. 3 of Part II of the rules do not apply to a case where the employer has failed to work within the maximum period prescribed by rr. 4 and 5 of Part III of the Act.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that he was in occupation of the premises as a tenant under the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 14(1)(a) of the Act. The High Court held that the provisions of section 15(1) of Act were applicable only to a case where the landlord had filed a written statement in the plaint and the same was not filed within the period prescribed by the Act, and therefore the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that section 15 (1) (a) was applicable only where the tenant had filed written statement within the time prescribed under the Act and not when he filed the written statement. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 15(2) are applicable only if the landlord has filed written statements in the suit and the written statements are filed within a period of three years from the date of filing of the written Statement. [782D] 2.1 In view of the language used in section 15, it is clear that the legislature intended to give retrospective effect to the provisions contained in Section 15 (2) of that Act only if there was a written agreement between the landlord and the tenant, that the landlord would be entitled to protection under section 14 (1)(b). [785D] 3.2 In view thereof, the High court erred in taking the view that the suit filed by the appellant for eviction on the basis of written statement was not maintainable because the provisions in Section 14(3) were applicable to a suit instituted after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed under section 15. [783E] 3:1 The provisions contained therein are applicable to suits instituted after a period specified in the Act or before any other date. In view, the provisions relating to suits filed by a landlord for eviction under Section 14 (3) are not applicable to such suits. [784G H; 784A B] 3 :2 The provisions in section 14 of the UP. Act are applicable even where there is a written contract between the parties and the landlord, that is, the date on which the suit is instituted. In the instant case, the appellant had filed the suit for ejectment on the strength of written statements within the prescribed period of two years from 1st April, 1974 to 31st March, 1975. The suit was filed after a lapse of more than three years and the suit having been filed beyond the period specified under section 16 (1), the suit would be barred by time. [882B C] 3.(a) In view the provisions made in Section 17(2)(a), it is not possible to hold that the plaintiff was entitled to relief under section 13 (1). The High court was right in holding, that since the appellant did not file written statement on the date fixed for filing of written Statement within the stipulated period of one year from 1.4.1975, he could not be allowed to take advantage of the provisions as contained in section 16(2). [784E] (b) In the absence of any written agreement or written statement, the suit could not have been filed within three years of the filing of such written statement and that the period for filing written statement would be extended from 1 st April, 1975 to 31.3.1975. The appellant was entitled only to the benefit under section 17(1).

The appellant was the tenant of a building in Calcutta. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he had no right to continue in possession of the land and that the appellant had not been given any right to remain in possession till the date of the suit. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit was barred by section 14 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to continue as a tenant under the West Premises Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1949 and that he was not entitled to remain on possession till he had been given an opportunity to defend his case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Act did not apply to the suit in view of section 14(1)(a) of the Act and that since the Act was a self contained code, the provisions of the Ordinance were not applicable to the suits in question. HELD: (i) The Act was not a self enacted code and it could not be applied to the proceedings in question as the Act had been passed by the Controller under section 14. [619 F] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that section 14 was applicable to a suit in which the Act came into force. [720 H; 720 A B] (iii) Section 14 of West Bengal Tenancy (Second Amendment) Ordinance 1949 did not make any provision for the eviction of tenants from land and the provisions contained therein were not attracted to the case. The Act had no application to the facts of the present case. [779 C D] (iv) The provisions of section 15 of the Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1947, which was in force on the date when the Act comes into force, could not apply even to a proceeding in which a decree for ejectment has been passed.

The appellant, a member of the Indian Administrative Service, was appointed as a Deputy Chief Engineer in the scale of Rs. 700 and was placed in the pay scale of ` 900. The Pay Commission recommended that the pay scales of the officers should be revised from time to time by the Government. The High Court held that the posts of Assistant Chief Engineers were not entitled to any higher pay than the scale prescribed for the post of Deputy Chief Engineers. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The pay scales are different from the pay of the employees in the grade of Deputy Divisional Engineer and the pay is fixed on the basis of the recommendations made by the Pay Commission. [703B] 2.2 The pay scale for the posts in the cadre of Deputy Conservator of Forests is a higher than that prescribed for them. It is not necessary to fix any pay scales for the officers working in the same grade. The pay structure of the officer is different from that prescribed by the Rules. The scale of pay is different and distinct from that of the post in which he is appointed. [774C D] 3.3 The pay of a person who has been appointed to a higher post is not a matter of right but a matter for consideration before the Pay Commis sioner. It cannot be said that the scale is different. The scales are distinct and separate from that which is the basis for fixing the pay. [764C] 4.4 In the instant case, the pay structure was revised by the State Government on the recommendations of the Pay Committee. The posts in question were not identical with the pay fixed for the purpose of fixing the scale. The post of Assistant Conservator of Forest was a higher grade and the scales were different from those which were given to the officers in the lower grade.

The respondent company was a Company incorporated under the Madhya Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation Act, 1956. The appellant company was carrying on business in the State of Madhya Bharat. It entered into an agreement with the respondent company for the supply of coal to the respondent Company. The respondent company paid tax at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per annum on the amount of tax payable by it under the provisions of the Act. The dispute between the parties was whether the respondent was liable to pay tax on the amounts of tax due from it under section 3(1) of the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1959. The State Government issued a notification under section 4(2) of that Act declaring the respondent liable to be assessed to tax under the Act and also for the levy of tax on coal. The High Court held that the respondent had no power to assess or collect tax under section 6 of the said Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the State Government had no authority to assess the tax under s.6 of the M.P. Municipalities Act and that the notification issued thereunder was ultra vires the Constitution as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the respondent 's liability to pay the tax was not disputed by the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notification is ultra vires Article 14 of its Constitution. [630 F] 2. The Act does not provide for any tax on land which has been assessed to a tax under this Act. It is not necessary that the tax should be levied in respect of any land which is assessed to an assessment under the MP. Municipal Act and the levy must be made by the State Legislature. [730 F G] 3. The notification issued under section 5(2)(a) of Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act is ultravires the Constitution. It does not contain any provision for the imposition of tax in respect thereof. The provisions of that section are not ultra vires article 14. [771 B C] 4. The power to levy tax on lands which have been assessed under the said section is subject to the control of the State legislature and it is only when the State Legislatures have made a law imposing a tax on such land that the imposition must be in respect whereof the tax has been levied. [764 D E] 5. The question whether the State Legislative Council was competent to levy a tax or not under the State Act is not one of fact. It cannot be said that the impugned notification issued by the Government under section 7(2), is ultra est. [751 F G; 771 A B] 6. The contention that the power to impose tax on property which has already been assessed and collected under the Central Act is a matter of legislative competence, is not correct. It was also contended that the Act does no more than provide for the collection of tax by the local authority. [784 D F] 7. The validity of the impugned notifications is challenged in this Court by special Leave. [ 771 B] 8. The contentions raised on behalf the appellant Company are : (i) that the provisions contained in section 6(2 ) of the Bhopal State Road Development Corporation Act and section 6 thereof are ultra vires Articles 14 and 19 of the constitution; (ii) that it is not open to the State legislatures to levy taxes on lands, which have already been collected under a Central Act. [791 D] 9.

The appellant was a lessee of the estate in which he was a tenant. The lease was granted to him on the ground that it had been executed by the Government under section 3(1) of the Madras Estates Land (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, as amended by the Madras Land Reforms (Amendment) Act of 1951, and the appellant was not entitled to any compensation for the period during which he had been in possession. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said section. The High Court held that the lease was not a lease within the meaning of section 3 (1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Act did not apply to the case because, as the Act had been passed by the State Government under the provisions of the Act, the Act could not be extended to the area in which the estate was situate. HELD : The Act is a piece of legislation and does not provide for any provision for compensation for termination of the lease. It is well settled that the legislature has intended to give effect to the intention of the legislature. But it cannot be said that the Legislature intended to confer a right on the lessee to terminate the lease, because, in the absence of any express provision or express provision, the statute would not have been applicable to the land in which it was situate and the Act would have no application to the present case. The Act does not contemplate any provision in the Act for compensation. It cannot be extended by a mere provision of law.
